It lists its NYSE- and NYSE Arca-registered common stock, preferred-stock depositary shares, and guaranteed notes and ETNs; reports no Section 12(g) securities; and provides required filing, filer-status, internal-control, error-correction, and shell-company disclosures. It also states market value and shares outstanding and incorporates specified 2025 proxy-statement portions for Part III items.

title: Form 10-K Index
summary: A Form 10-K index listing Parts I–IV and page references. It covers the company’s business, segments, competition, regulation, human capital and asset/liability distribution; risk factors, staff comments, properties, legal proceedings and mine safety; stock information, management discussion, market risks, financial statements, accounting matters, controls and disclosures; directors, compensation, ownership, related-party matters and auditor fees; and exhibits and financial statement schedules.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business.
JPMorganChase Overview and Business Segments
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase is a Delaware-based global financial services firm with $4.0 trillion in assets and $344.8 billion in equity at year-end 2024, serving consumer, business, institutional and government clients. The text describes its principal U.S. bank and broker-dealer subsidiaries, international operations, and free online access to SEC filings and company information, noting website content is not incorporated into the Form 10-K. From the second quarter of 2024, its reportable segments are Consumer & Community Banking, Commercial & Investment Bank, and Asset & Wealth Management; remaining activities are in Corporate. Segment and Corporate details appear in the MD&A and Note 32.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase competes in highly competitive markets against a wide range of financial and nonfinancial firms, including banks, investment and insurance companies, fintechs, and internet businesses. Competition is based on product and service quality and variety, execution, innovation, reputation, and price, and differs by client, industry, geography, and whether competition is global, national, or regional. New online-only and nonfinancial entrants also challenge traditional banking services.

nodes.title: Supervision and regulation
Financial holding company:
key_items: Consolidated supervision; Permissible business activities; Capital and liquidity requirements
Enhanced prudential standards; Holding company as a source of strength; Regulation of acquisitions; Ongoing obligations
Holding company as a source of strength
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase is extensively regulated in the U.S. and abroad. The Federal Reserve oversees the holding company on a consolidated basis, while bank, broker-dealer, derivatives and foreign subsidiaries face oversight from relevant U.S., U.K., EU, German and local regulators. U.S. law limits BHC activities, permits broader FHC activities subject to eligibility and CRA conditions, and allows restrictions or corrective action. Regulators set capital, liquidity and leverage requirements; proposed U.S. Basel III revisions and EU/U.K. implementation timelines remain relevant. The Firm and its bank conduct annual supervisory and company-run stress tests, submit capital plans, and face SCB determinations; proposed framework changes and litigation are noted. Enhanced prudential rules require risk and liquidity controls and board oversight, and the parent must support depository subsidiaries. Acquisitions are subject to approval, notice, concentration limits and eligibility rules. The Firm also has continuing CFTC cooperation obligations and 2024 regulatory orders and resolution concerning trading-venue inventories and surveillance data.

nodes.title: Subsidiary banks:
key_items: FDIC deposit insurance; FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
Heightened Supervisory Standards; Restrictions on transactions with affiliates; Dividend restrictions; Depositor preference
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory obligations: national-bank powers and OCC enforcement; FDIC insurance funding, insolvency powers, capital-correction rules, heightened governance standards, affiliate-transaction and dividend limits, and depositor priority. It covers U.S. and U.K. consumer supervision, including CFPB rules on card late fees, data sharing and overdrafts, proposed debit interchange limits, and U.K. conduct requirements. It also summarizes broker-dealer and market-conduct regulation, investment-management and fiduciary rules, derivatives oversight and requirements, and introduces global data, privacy, cybersecurity and AI regulation.

nodes.title: Financial Services Regulatory Overview
nodes.summary: The page describes U.K. retail banking and investment services regulation, including prudential, conduct, payment-systems and consumer-protection oversight. It outlines securities and broker-dealer regulation in the U.S. and abroad, covering business practices, capital, records and market conduct. It summarizes asset and wealth management rules on client assets, funds, fiduciary duties and evolving standards, including the stayed 2024 U.S. DOL fiduciary rule. It also details U.S., EU, U.K. and other derivatives requirements, including registration, capital, collateral, clearing, trading, conduct, reporting and anti-manipulation rules.

nodes.title: Data, privacy, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence regulation:
nodes.summary: The Firm faces evolving global regulation affecting data privacy, cybersecurity and AI, including EU DORA requirements from January 2025 and phased AI Act rules from February 2025. It must meet anti-money-laundering, reporting and customer due-diligence obligations under the BSA, and comply with U.S., EU, U.K. and other sanctions regimes, including potentially conflicting laws. Anti-corruption laws apply globally. U.S. and international regulators oversee compensation practices to limit imprudent risk-taking, with rules continuing to evolve. EU sustainability rules CSRD and CSDDD impose expanded reporting, human-rights and environmental due diligence, and climate-plan duties on phased schedules, affecting EU and non-EU entities. Industry groups are litigating regulations, including a December 2024 challenge to the Federal Reserve’s stress-testing process.

nodes.title: Regulatory and Sustainability Requirements
key_items: The Bank Secrecy Act and Economic Sanctions:
nodes.summary: The text describes evolving regulations affecting the Firm, including EU requirements for ICT resilience and artificial intelligence. It covers anti-money-laundering controls, recordkeeping and due diligence under the Bank Secrecy Act; U.S., EU, U.K. and other economic sanctions; anti-corruption laws; regulator oversight of compensation and risk-taking; and expanding sustainability reporting and due diligence rules, including CSRD and CSDDD requirements for ESG disclosures, human rights, environmental impacts and climate transition plans.

nodes.title: Litigation and regulatory challenges:
nodes.summary: Financial-industry trade groups have filed lawsuits challenging regulations that could increase financial institutions’ costs or harm operations: the BPI, U.S. Chamber of Commerce and others contest the Federal Reserve’s stress-testing process; trade groups challenge the CFPB late-fee rule, which is stayed pending litigation; the CFPB data-sharing rule; and the overdraft rule, for which the CFPB agreed in part to a 90-day effective-date delay and temporary litigation stay, both awaiting court approval. Groups also challenged the DOL fiduciary rule, whose effective date two courts stayed in July 2024.

Describes JPMorgan Chase’s extensive U.S. and international supervision of its holding company and subsidiaries, including activity and acquisition limits, capital, liquidity, stress testing, governance, resolution support and regulatory enforcement. Covers bank, consumer, broker-dealer, investment-management, fiduciary and derivatives requirements; data privacy, cybersecurity, AI, AML, sanctions, anti-corruption, compensation and sustainability rules. It also notes evolving implementation and regulatory orders, plus industry litigation challenging stress-testing, CFPB and DOL rules.

nodes.title: Human Capital
key_items: Attracting and retaining employees; Developing employees
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase says long-term success depends on attracting, developing and retaining talent in an inclusive workplace; figures exclude contractors. At year-end 2024 it had 317,233 employees across 66 countries, up 7,307, mainly in front-office and technology roles; 59% were in the U.S. The text gives workforce breakdowns by region and business line, and self-identified demographic data for employees, senior staff, the Operating Committee and directors, with definitions, coverage and exclusions. It describes recruitment and internal mobility (56% of 2024 openings filled externally), required and voluntary training, leadership development, performance- and risk-conscious compensation, and location-dependent benefits and wellness support.

JPMorganChase’s business section describes its global operations, financial scale, subsidiaries, online information and three reportable segments, with other activities in Corporate. It outlines competition from financial, fintech and other firms; extensive U.S. and international regulation of its businesses, activities, risk, governance and conduct; and evolving rules and related litigation. It also covers its 2024 workforce’s size, locations, business and demographic composition, and its approaches to recruitment, mobility, training, development, compensation, benefits and wellness.

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors.
Summary
Summary (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase warns that the listed material risks are not exhaustive and could individually or collectively harm its business, earnings, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness, or reputation. Risks include regulatory and legal changes, costs, penalties and resolution losses; political and country instability; market volatility; borrower and counterparty credit losses; liquidity and funding pressures; capital requirements; operational, technology, cyber, privacy, vendor, control and model failures; ineffective strategy, competition and climate impacts; employee conduct and retention; and reputational damage from misconduct, failures, litigation, conflicts, fiduciary shortcomings or unmet ESG expectations. Detailed risk disclosures govern.

nodes.title: Regulatory
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase operates worldwide under extensive, evolving laws and regulatory supervision that shape its business and may require operational changes, creating costs, reducing revenue and profitability, or complicating new ventures and business initiatives. Restrictions such as limits on consumer fees could prompt product changes, resource reallocation and restructuring. Regulatory requirements may also force the firm to limit offerings or market-making liquidity, forgo opportunities, pay higher taxes or charges, absorb fraud losses, sell assets disadvantageously, restrict activities, or raise prices and reduce demand. Noncompliance may bring greater scrutiny, enforcement, fines or sanctions, litigation exposure, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s businesses are highly regulated, and the laws, rules and regulations that apply to JPMorganChase have a significant impact on its business and operations.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks involving business-strategy effectiveness; employee conduct and its effects on reputation and stakeholder relationships; country conditions and geopolitical conflict; attracting and retaining staff amid immigration or travel-policy changes; and litigation or investigations. It then explains that JPMorganChase operates under extensive, evolving global regulation that can require operational changes, raise costs, reduce revenues, constrain initiatives and consumer products, or prompt restructuring. Regulatory responses may include limiting services or market-making liquidity, forgoing opportunities, paying higher taxes or charges, incurring losses, selling assets, restricting activities, or raising prices. Noncompliance may lead to scrutiny, enforcement, sanctions, litigation, and reputational harm.

nodes.title: Differences and inconsistencies in financial services regulation and supervision can negatively impact JPMorganChase’s businesses, operations and financial results.
nodes.summary: Differences in financial regulation and supervision by firm size, competitor type, and jurisdiction may give JPMorganChase’s less-regulated or locally favored competitors advantages, particularly in unregulated products. Inconsistent implementation of global standards, stricter national rules, and conflicting cross-border laws can create compliance risks and require operational or legal-entity changes, including local subsidiaries, capital and liquidity, ring-fencing, resolution, clearing, derivatives, governance, conduct, and compensation measures. Resulting impacts may include restructuring or divestitures, higher capital, compliance and operating costs, price or product changes, foregone opportunities, and sanctions, harming competitiveness, operations, results, and profitability.

nodes.title: Resolving regulatory investigations can subject JPMorganChase to significant penalties and collateral consequences, and could result in higher compliance costs or restrictions on its operations.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and has incurred significant fines and other consequences from investigations; future resolutions may raise compliance and operating costs or restrict operations. Required admissions of wrongdoing can increase litigation exposure, harm its reputation, and limit business opportunities. Criminal actions or guilty pleas may cause customer losses, product or service restrictions, or loss of operating permissions. The company expects continued scrutiny, punitive formal enforcement, and greater enforcement risk due to prior actions. Failure to meet resolution terms or regulatory standards could bring further penalties, judgments, restrictions, management changes, sanctions, prosecution, or litigation. Investigations involving acquired businesses, investments, joint ventures, or vendors may also increase costs or capital requirements.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s operations and financial results can be negatively impacted in jurisdictions with less predictable legal and regulatory frameworks.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from unpredictable legal and regulatory environments, including inconsistent laws, government actions, corruption, arbitrary proceedings, and license or relationship termination, which can impair operations and earnings, as illustrated by Russian litigation and asset seizures. Such jurisdictions require added compliance resources and heighten noncompliance risk. Conflicting government policies discouraging or penalizing business with certain industries, or mandating practices, can cause restrictions, enforcement threats, and reputational harm. Resolution-plan requirements may drive restructuring, divestitures, higher costs, or business constraints; resolution-plan deficiencies can trigger stricter requirements. Parent-company eligible long-term debt must help recapitalize subsidiaries in bankruptcy or FDIC receivership, exposing debt and equity holders to losses.

nodes.title: Legal, Governmental and Resolution Risks
key_items: JPMorganChase's businesses may be negatively impacted by governmental policies that either discourage or penalize business with certain industries or require specific business practices.

Requirements for the orderly resolution of JPMorganChase could result in JPMorganChase having to restructure or reorganize its businesses and could increase its funding or operational costs or curtail its businesses.
nodes.summary: Unpredictable legal and regulatory frameworks may cause litigation, asset seizures, license or relationship losses, compliance costs, operational disruption and reduced earnings. Government policies discouraging or penalizing business with certain industries, or mandating practices, may create conflicting obligations, restrictions, enforcement threats and reputational harm. Resolution-plan requirements may force JPMorganChase to change its structure or activities, raise costs, constrain growth or client service, or restructure, reorganize or divest businesses.

nodes.title: Holders of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s debt and equity securities will absorb losses if it were to enter into a resolution.
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase’s debt and equity holders may absorb losses in a resolution. Federal Reserve rules require the Parent Company to maintain eligible long-term debt and loss-absorbing capacity. Under the preferred single-point-of-entry strategy, equity holders bear losses first, then unsecured creditors, whose claims rank behind subsidiary creditors and the Parent Company’s secured and priority creditors; recovery depends on residual subsidiary value. The FDIC may use a similar approach under Title II but has not committed to it, and authorities need not follow the company’s preferred plan. Political and geopolitical developments—including monetary and fiscal policies, isolationism, sanctions, tariffs, immigration, and health-emergency responses—may raise uncertainty and volatility, undermine confidence, provoke retaliation or cyberattacks, disrupt government funding, affect policy and clients, and deter business. Possible outcomes include slower growth, inflation, recession, labor disruption, and greater market volatility.

nodes.title: Political
nodes.summary: The text explains that under JPMorganChase’s preferred single-point-of-entry resolution, Parent Company equity holders would absorb losses first, followed by unsecured creditors, including eligible LTD holders; their claims rank behind subsidiary creditors and Parent Company secured and priority creditors, and recovery depends on residual subsidiary value. The FDIC has indicated this model may be expected under Title II but has made no commitment, and authorities need not follow it, potentially increasing losses. It also describes how U.S. and global political or geopolitical developments—including monetary and fiscal policy, protectionism, sanctions, immigration, and health-emergency responses—may create economic and market uncertainty, weaken confidence, raise cyber and government-funding risks, affect policy and counterparties, constrain business opportunities, and contribute to slower growth, inflation, recession, labor disruption, and volatility.

nodes.title: Economic uncertainty or instability caused by political and geopolitical developments can negatively impact JPMorganChase’s businesses.
nodes.summary: The text explains Parent Company resolution: under JPMorganChase’s preferred single-point-of-entry plan, equity absorbs losses first, then unsecured creditors, including eligible LTD holders, whose recovery is subordinate to subsidiary, secured and statutory-priority claims. The FDIC expects a similar approach but has not committed to one; authorities need not follow JPMorganChase’s plan, and losses could be greater. It also outlines how political, geopolitical, economic and market developments can disrupt confidence, growth, markets, credit, operations and supply chains, causing losses, liquidity or capital declines, higher credit costs, and weaker results or ratings. Consumer businesses are especially exposed to employment, income, interest rates, housing and collateral values, inflation, confidence, spending and debt, which affect credit performance and demand.

nodes.title: Economic and Market Risks
key_items: Economic and market events and conditions can materially affect JPMorganChase’s businesses and investment and market-making positions.
nodes.summary: The page explains how economic, market, political, regulatory and extraordinary events can harm JPMorganChase. Risks include adverse sentiment, economic conditions, rates, prices, credit and liquidity; geopolitical conflict, cyberattacks, climate and health emergencies; currency movements, reduced investment, debt and securities sales, supply-chain disruptions, and changes to political or economic alliances. Unexpected losses, credit events, correlations or ineffective hedging may affect trading and investment positions. Consequences can include lower profits, liquidity and capital, higher credit losses, impaired client services, constrained business growth, and weaker financial condition or credit ratings.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s consumer businesses can be negatively affected by adverse economic conditions and governmental policies.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s consumer businesses are vulnerable to U.S. and global economic conditions, including income and employment, interest rates, collateral and housing values, inflation, confidence, spending, and consumer debt. Weak conditions can reduce demand and borrowers’ ability to repay, increasing delinquencies, credit-loss allowances, and charge-offs and lowering earnings, with greater impacts in areas facing industrial decline or heavy consumer debt. Government policies affecting health insurance, education, immigration, housing, employment, financial-service fees, taxes, or regulation may also reduce consumer income or harm earnings.

nodes.title: Unfavorable market and economic conditions can have an adverse effect on JPMorganChase’s wholesale businesses.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks to JPMorganChase from unfavorable markets and economic conditions: lower wholesale transaction and capital-markets fees, underwriting losses and unsold credit commitments; reduced asset-management and custody fees, client outflows and fund performance impacts; sector stress and commercial-real-estate weakness causing borrower distress, credit losses, servicing costs, operational, regulatory and reputational risks. Interest-rate changes can affect income, lending, deposits, securities values, funding, liquidity, capital, loan performance, margins and mortgage-servicing rights; wider credit spreads affect borrowing costs and fair-value liabilities. Market volatility and illiquidity can impair financial-instrument valuations and produce losses despite risk controls and hedges. Finally, client, counterparty, custodian and clearinghouse financial deterioration can expose the firm to credit losses, disputes and litigation.

nodes.title: Interest Rate, Market and Credit Risks
key_items: Changes in interest rates and credit spreads can adversely affect JPMorganChase’s earnings, its liquidity or its capital levels.
JPMorganChase’s results may be materially affected by market fluctuations and significant changes in the valuation of financial instruments.
nodes.summary: The page describes how changing interest rates and credit spreads can affect JPMorganChase’s earnings, liquidity, capital, funding costs, deposits, lending, securities, and mortgage servicing rights, including risks to borrowers with variable-rate loans. Market volatility and illiquidity can make financial instruments difficult to value, cause losses on disposal, and undermine risk-management strategies. Credit risk arises from clients, counterparties, custodians, and central counterparties, potentially leading to losses, disputes, or litigation after defaults.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase can be negatively affected by adverse changes in the financial condition of clients, counterparties, custodians and CCPs.
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorganChase’s risks from interest rates and credit spreads: rising rates may boost net interest income but can reduce lending, trigger credit losses, deposit outflows, AFS securities losses, funding costs and liquidity pressures, and impair variable-rate borrowers; low or negative rates can compress margins, alter depositor behavior and reduce mortgage-servicing-rights value. Wider credit spreads affect borrowing costs and fair-value liabilities. Market volatility and illiquidity can make instruments difficult to value or sell, causing losses despite risk controls and hedging. Credit risks include defaults or failures of clients, counterparties, custodians and CCPs; inadequate collateral, clearing and intraday exposures, disputes, sovereign actions, legal limits, and cascading market disruption can produce losses, costs, investigations and reputational harm. Foreclosed-property governance or control deficiencies may also invite regulatory scrutiny and reputational damage.

JPMorganChase warns that its risks, individually or together, may harm its business, earnings, financial condition, capital, liquidity, competitiveness, or reputation. Risks include extensive and inconsistent global regulation; investigations, penalties, litigation, unpredictable legal regimes, and resolution requirements; political and geopolitical instability; adverse economic, market, interest-rate, and credit conditions; and borrower, counterparty, custodian, and clearinghouse failures. Regulatory, political, and economic developments can constrain business, raise costs, disrupt operations and markets, and weaken consumer and wholesale businesses. Operational, technology, cyber, privacy, vendor, control, model, strategy, climate, employee, conduct, and reputational risks are also identified. In resolution, Parent Company equity and then unsecured creditors may absorb losses; authorities may not follow the firm’s preferred plan. Detailed disclosures govern.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase may suffer losses if the value of collateral declines in stressed market conditions.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s credit risk and potential losses may rise during market stress or illiquidity if collateral loses value, cannot be realized at its estimated or fair value, is liquidated for less than the amount owed, or counterparties cannot post it. Disputes over collateral valuations may also increase, making losses more likely.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase could incur significant losses arising from concentrations of credit and market risk.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces losses from concentrated or interconnected credit and market exposures, contagion across related industries and regions, regulatory reserve requirements, competitors’ excessive consumer lending, consumer defaults, and inability to reduce positions during market disruptions, which can raise risk-weighted assets and hurt capital, funding costs, and profits. Liquidity may be constrained by market disruption, regulation, government actions, asset-sale limits, participant defaults, unexpected outflows, or lost confidence; costly alternative funding and liquidity requirements may further impair operations. The holding company depends on restricted subsidiary dividends and loans to service securities, pay dividends, redeem securities, and meet obligations, potentially triggering earlier insolvency or resolution.

nodes.title: Reductions in JPMorganChase’s credit ratings may adversely affect its liquidity and cost of funding.

Maintaining the required level and composition of capital may impact JPMorganChase’s ability to support business activities, meet evolving regulatory requirements and distribute capital to shareholders.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from credit-rating downgrades, which could limit JPMorganChase’s market access, raise funding and collateral costs, reduce counterparties and investors, constrain business, and affect debt values. It describes rating factors and monitoring. It also covers regulatory capital requirements and possible increases, their effects on buybacks, dividends, capital instruments and operations, and uncertainty around proposed Basel III and GSIB rules. Finally, it explains reliance on internal and third-party operational systems, past and potential outages and customer impacts, and growing challenges from complexity, fraud, errors, and undetected weaknesses.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s businesses are dependent on the effectiveness of internal and external operational systems.
nodes.summary: The text describes capital risks from balance-sheet changes, higher risk-weighted assets or stress losses, and potential consequences of failing to meet capital requirements, including limits on buybacks, capital instruments, dividends, or business activity. Proposed Basel III and GSIB surcharge rules may affect capital and business decisions. It also details operational-system dependencies, including data quality, maintenance, security, third-party providers, cyber threats, human and technical failures, and growing interconnectivity. Disruptions can harm customers, impede transactions and services, cause losses, costs, litigation, sanctions, market-wide effects and reputational damage, potentially materially affecting JPMorganChase.

nodes.title: A successful cyber attack affecting JPMorganChase could cause significant harm to JPMorganChase and its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces frequent, increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks from varied actors, including malware, data theft or manipulation, service disruption, ransomware, and attacks on online and third-party services. Past and future breaches may be difficult to anticipate, detect, prevent, investigate, contain, or remediate, given evolving threats, limited control over external systems, digital and cloud expansion, AI and quantum advances, acquisitions, and insider risks. Ongoing cybersecurity investment and controls are essential; failures could cause operational disruption, data loss, fraud, ransom demands, financial and reputational damage, customer distrust, uninsured losses, litigation, and regulatory penalties. Investigations may delay disclosure and allow harm to spread or recur.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase can be negatively affected if it fails to identify and address operational risks associated with the introduction of or changes to products, services and delivery platforms or the adoption of new technologies.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase may suffer operational risks when launching or changing products, services, delivery platforms, or technologies, or through acquisitions and investments. It may fail to identify risks—such as greater reliance on third parties—or implement adequate controls. Significant failures could disrupt operations and lead to client or counterparty liability, increased compliance, operational, integration, or litigation costs, regulatory sanctions or intervention, reputational damage, impaired liquidity, and weaker competitiveness, materially harming its business and results.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s business and operations rely on its ability, and the ability of key external parties, to maintain appropriately-staffed workforces, and on the competence, trustworthiness, health and safety of employees.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s efficient operations, profitability, customer offerings, and risk management depend on appropriately staffed, competent, trustworthy, healthy, and safe employees, as well as the workforces of vendors, custodians, market infrastructures, and potential acquisitions. Operations may be harmed by poor business decisions, inadequate risk controls or training, staffing shortages, workforce unavailability during health emergencies or extraordinary events, operational failures, theft, fraud, unlawful conduct, human error, or misconduct. Ineffective employee-protection measures by JPMorganChase, authorities, or relied-upon external parties may also impair operations.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase faces substantial legal and operational risks in the processing and safeguarding of personal information.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces privacy and data-protection risks from complex, changing global laws, enforcement, conflicting jurisdictional requirements, and inadequate controls among external parties. Compliance may raise costs, require management oversight and inefficient systems, and constrain products, services, and data transfers. Mishandling, unauthorized disclosure, interception, or AI-enabled identity fraud could cause litigation, sanctions, losses, reputational harm, and client or employee attrition. Regulatory scrutiny may prompt stricter rules, including cross-border restrictions and local data storage or processing, further increasing costs and limiting operations and offerings.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s operations, results and reputation could be harmed by occurrences of extraordinary events beyond its control.
nodes.summary: Extraordinary events beyond JPMorganChase’s control—including cyberattacks, physical security incidents, outages, system or provider failures, property damage, climate change, disasters, accidents, health crises, unrest, hostilities and terrorism—could disrupt operations and damage its reputation. The firm’s resiliency framework aims to prepare for, withstand and recover from disruptions affecting critical functions and supporting people, technology, data and facilities, but cannot guarantee protection, especially against simultaneous, prolonged, geographically concentrated or increasingly chronic events. Disruptions could impede services and transactions, require costly remediation, cause losses or liabilities, affect market infrastructure, trigger litigation or regulatory sanctions, and harm reputation. They could also weaken clients’ and customers’ financial condition or creditworthiness, increasing delinquencies, credit-loss allowances and charge-offs and reducing earnings.

nodes.title: Data quality is essential to JPMorganChase’s business and operations, and if JPMorganChase fails to maintain adequate data management processes, this could adversely affect its ability to effectively manage its businesses, comply with applicable laws, rules and regulations, or remain competitive.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase depends on accurate, timely, complete and secure data to manage risk; detect fraud and cyber threats; develop analytical, machine-learning and AI models; maintain compliance; and prepare financial and regulatory reporting. Weak data processes—including problems with collection, analysis, validation or safeguarding—could undermine risk management, reporting, compliance, market-making, liquidity and capital decisions, client services and fraud prevention. Consequences may include poor decisions, higher costs, operational failures, regulatory breaches, customer harm and reputational damage.

nodes.title: Enhanced regulatory and other standards for the oversight of vendors and other service providers can result in higher costs and other potential exposures.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces enhanced regulatory and other standards for overseeing vendors and service providers, including outsourced functions and significant functions performed by subsidiaries. Addressing related risks incurs significant costs. Failure to assess and manage these relationships, particularly those involving critical banking functions, shared services, or other activities, could materially harm the company through customer harm and liability, regulatory sanctions, lost revenue and opportunity costs, increased operating costs, and reputational damage.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s risk management framework and control environment will not be effective in identifying and mitigating every risk to JPMorganChase.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s risk framework and controls cannot identify or mitigate every risk. Deficiencies in governance, practices, models, reporting or controls could cause unexpected losses and materially harm financial results, delay escalation, prompt poor decisions, require costly remediation, cause legal or regulatory noncompliance and scrutiny, litigation, fines or sanctions, customer harm, reputational damage, and reduced confidence. Risk strategies rely partly on historical behavior and subjective assumptions; correlations may shift during market stress or unforeseen events, while sudden market or economic changes can undermine these strategies and cause losses.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase could recognize unexpected losses, its capital levels could be reduced and it could face greater regulatory scrutiny if its models, estimations or judgments, including those used in its financial statements, are inadequate or incorrect.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase uses models, estimates and judgments—including AI and machine learning—for risk management, stress testing and financial reporting. These may fail because of unreliable historical data or assumptions, forecasting limits, market illiquidity, technology or data errors, inadequate reviews, or bias. Inaccurate models can cause unexpected losses, uncertainty in valuations and credit-loss allowances, reduced capital and greater regulatory scrutiny. Regulators must approve certain models used for Basel III risk-weighted assets; rejection may increase capital charges, harm results or constrain business growth.

nodes.title: Lapses, weaknesses or deficiencies in controls over disclosure or financial reporting could materially affect JPMorganChase’s profitability or reputation.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces risks from ineffective disclosure controls or weaknesses in financial reporting amid complex, changing regulations. These could cause inaccurate reports, harming business, operations, financial condition, market access, reputation and investor confidence, or leading to remediation costs, litigation and sanctions. Its results and competitive position also depend on management choosing and executing sound strategies across offerings, markets, clients, acquisitions, counterparties, technologies, and distribution methods. Poor or misinformed choices, or failure to adapt to competition, regulation, markets and stakeholder expectations, could damage franchise value, growth prospects and earnings; effective near- and long-term business plans are also essential.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase’s results or competitive standing could suffer if its management fails to develop and execute effective business strategies, and to anticipate changes affecting those strategies.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces risks from biased or inaccurate models and judgments used in risk management, valuations, and credit-loss estimates; regulatory rejection of models could increase capital charges and constrain business growth. Weak disclosure or financial-reporting controls could cause inaccurate reporting, financial harm, restricted market access, remediation costs, litigation or penalties, reputational damage, and reduced investor confidence. Strategic performance may suffer if management fails to choose and execute effective plans, adapt to competition and changing expectations or regulations, allocate capital and monitor investments wisely, conduct due diligence and integrate acquisitions, address stakeholder and ESG concerns, respond to market shifts, or develop needed capabilities; disposing of excess facilities may also be costly.

nodes.title: JPMorganChase faces significant and increasing competition in the rapidly evolving financial services industry.
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase faces intensifying U.S. and global competition from banks, financial firms, technology companies and other nonbanks amid regulatory, technological, public-scrutiny and economic change. New entrants and digital services—including online trading, lending, payments, automated investment advice, cryptocurrencies and distributed ledgers—may disrupt traditional banking and require costly adaptation; security and compliance risks may further raise costs and reduce income. Aggressive nonbank lending could erode market share and worsen downturns. Competition may pressure prices, reduce share and revenues if products fail to meet customer expectations, and require additional investment or capital for clients; adverse effects on results cannot be ruled out.

nodes.title: The effects of climate change could adversely affect JPMorganChase’s business and operations, both directly and as a result of impacts on its clients and customers.
nodes.summary: Climate change may harm JPMorganChase directly and through its clients, customers, markets and business strategy. Physical risks include severe weather and chronic climate shifts, potentially reducing asset values and insurance availability, disrupting operations and supply chains, and driving migration or unemployment. Transition risks from policy, technology and consumer changes may strand assets, raise compliance and energy costs, undermine business models and damage reputation. Conflicting regional rules and uncertain climate data and models may also cause inaccurate disclosures or reporting. nodes.title: Firmwide Risk Management
Risk governance framework
key_items: Three lines of defense; Risk identification and ownership
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes risk as inherent to its activities and aims to balance client, customer and investor interests with the Firm’s safety and soundness. Effective management requires individual accountability and escalation, risk ownership in each business and corporate area, firmwide governance, and risk-aware compensation under Board oversight. Its framework covers risk drivers (including economic, regulatory, business, human, market and natural factors), four risk types—strategic, credit and investment, market, and operational—and quantitative and qualitative impacts such as losses, liquidity outflows, penalties, reputational harm and regulatory action. Independent Risk Management, led by the CRO with Board Risk Committee approval, sets and oversees governance through firmwide and business risk executives and the Chief Compliance Officer. The three lines of defense are business units and specified functions that own risks and controls; IRM, which independently measures, assesses and challenges risk; and Internal Audit, which independently evaluates governance and controls. Other corporate functions also manage risks in their areas. Businesses identify, control, catalog and regularly review material risks; IRM challenges and consolidates them for committee and Board review. Quantitative and qualitative risk appetite is periodically set by senior management, approved by the Board Risk Committee, monitored, measured and reported.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight structure
nodes.summary: Describes the Firm’s independent risk governance structure and escalation channels to senior management, the Firmwide Risk Committee, and the Board. The Board and its independent committees oversee risk, controls, compensation and succession, public responsibility, and corporate governance; the Operating Committee escalates information to the Board. Management committees oversee firmwide, business, regional, control, asset-liability, and valuation risks. The text also lists risk oversight functions covered in subsequent sections, including strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, credit, investment, market, country, climate, operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and model-estimation risks.

nodes.title: Risk governance and oversight functions
nodes.summary: Line of Business and Corporate Function Control Committees review emerging and elevated operational, compliance and conduct risks, address control concerns, and oversee remediation. ALCO oversees asset and liability management, including balance-sheet, liquidity, interest-rate and capital-risk frameworks. The senior-executive Valuation Governance Forum oversees risks from firmwide valuation activities. The text introduces the Firm’s risk governance and oversight functions, noting that activities may span multiple risk drivers, types and impacts, and lists the covered functions: strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, consumer and wholesale credit, investment portfolio, market, country, climate, operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation and model risk, with page references.

nodes.title: Strategic Risk Management
Management and oversight
nodes.summary: The text defines strategic risk and describes its management: senior business leaders and the Operating Committee manage major risks, IRM participates in reviews and assesses initiatives, and the Board oversees strategy and risk governance. Periodically updated strategic plans incorporate risk appetite, budgets, capital, earnings, and asset-liability objectives; the Board reviews and approves them, while balance-sheet strategy emphasizes risk-adjusted returns, capital, and liquidity. Capital risk is defined, and the Firm’s fortress-balance-sheet approach, independent capital-risk oversight, Treasury and CIO capital-management objectives and processes, and governance committees are outlined. Capital planning includes annual Board-approved regulatory plans and Federal Reserve CCAR stress testing of capital adequacy, internal assessment, and distributions.

nodes.title: Capital Risk Management
Capital planning and stress testing
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s capital-risk philosophy: maintaining strong, stable capital and liquidity to support business and withstand stress, with senior management evaluating capital impacts of major decisions. An independent Capital Risk Management function oversees metrics, limits, breaches, management assessments, and regulatory compliance; Treasury and CIO manage capital to support investment, flexibility, subsidiaries, regulatory requirements, distributions, and resolution readiness. Governance involves management committees and Board review. It describes annual Federal Reserve CCAR requirements, the 3.3% stress capital buffer through September 30, 2025, and 12.3% standardized CET1 requirement at year-end 2024. The annual ICAAP integrates capital planning and stress tests across macroeconomic, market, and operational scenarios, with Audit Committee oversight and tailored analyses as needed.

nodes.title: Contingency Capital Plan
nodes.summary: The Contingency Capital Plan establishes the Firm’s capital management framework and principles in normal and stressed conditions. It explains how target capital levels are calibrated and minimum requirements met, how planned distributions are monitored for continued appropriateness, and what contingency actions may be taken or considered at different levels of capital depletion during stress.

nodes.title: Regulatory capital
Basel III Overview
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve sets consolidated capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase & Co., while the OCC sets similar requirements for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; U.S. rules generally follow Basel standards. Basel III requires minimum capital ratios based on risk-weighted assets (RWA), calculated using Standardized and Advanced approaches, with the Firm assessed against the more binding approach’s requirements. Credit-risk RWA relies mainly on supervisory risk weights under Standardized and internal models under Advanced; market-risk calculations are generally consistent, while Advanced also includes operational risk. Management may adjust RWA using judgment and regulatory feedback. At year-end 2024, Standardized risk-based ratios were more binding, and the Firm must also calculate the supplementary leverage ratio (SLR).

nodes.title: Key Regulatory Developments U.S. Basel III Finalization
nodes.summary: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC proposed amendments to the risk-based capital framework for large banking organizations and those with significant trading activity, called the U.S. Basel III proposal in the Form 10-K. It would replace the Advanced approach with an expanded risk-based approach for calculating risk-weighted assets and apply the stress capital buffer requirement to both the expanded risk-based and Standardized approaches.

nodes.title: GSIB Surcharge and TLAC and Eligible LTD Requirements
nodes.summary: In July 2023, the Federal Reserve proposed changing the GSIB surcharge calculation to use annual averages of quarterly calculations, with daily averaging for certain measures, reduce surcharge increments from 50 to 10 basis points, and make technical changes to Method 2. These changes would revise risk-based capital requirements for U.S. GSIBs. In August 2023, the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC proposed extending eligible long-term debt and clean holding company requirements to non-GSIB banks with at least $100 billion in assets, limiting shorter-maturity debt counted toward GSIB TLAC, and expanding capital deductions to cover non-GSIB issuers. Finalization and implementation dates are uncertain; the Firm monitors developments and potential impacts.

nodes.title: Risk-based Capital Regulatory Requirements
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Firm’s Basel III capital requirements: the 4.5% minimum CET1 ratio plus conservation buffers, including fixed or variable components, GSIB surcharge, and countercyclical buffer. It explains the two annual GSIB assessment methods, reports 2023–2024 surcharges, and notes 2025 rates remain 2.5% under Method 1 and 4.5% under Method 2. The countercyclical buffer was 0% at year-end 2024 and may rise by up to 2.5%. Capital shortfalls restrict distributions and certain bonuses. The text also covers TLAC and eligible debt requirements, the 3.0% SLR minimum and additional 2.0% buffer, consequences of SLR shortfalls, and separate well-capitalized requirements for the Firm and its bank subsidiary, with references to further disclosures.

nodes.title: TLAC and Supplementary Leverage Requirements
key_items: Leverage-based Capital Regulatory Requirements Supplementary leverage ratio
nodes.summary: The Federal Reserve requires U.S. GSIB top-tier holding companies, including the Firm, to maintain minimum external TLAC and eligible long-term debt. Basel III Advanced Approach organizations must maintain a 3.0% minimum supplementary leverage ratio (SLR), with the Firm and certain others also subject to a 2.0% leverage buffer. SLR is Tier 1 capital divided by total leverage exposure, comprising adjusted average on-balance-sheet assets plus specified off-balance-sheet exposures. Falling below the required SLR limits capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, and certain executive bonuses.

nodes.title: Other regulatory capital

Note 27 provides details on capital ratios and applicable U.S. federal standards; the Firm’s website publishes Pillar 3 disclosures with current capital measures.

nodes.title: Liquidity Risk Management
Internal stress testing
nodes.summary: The text defines liquidity risk and outlines its oversight by the independent Liquidity Risk Management function, which sets and monitors metrics, limits, breaches, processes, stress tests, and assumptions. Treasury and CIO manage liquidity by assessing balance-sheet characteristics and restrictions, maintaining stress assumptions, strategies, contingency plans and regulatory compliance, managing limits and funds-transfer pricing, and centrally optimizing liquidity while monitoring exposures and transfer constraints. Governance involves firmwide and regional ALCOs, the Treasurer Committee, CTC Risk Committee, and Board Risk Committee. Daily and event-driven stress tests model funding access, contingent outflows, downgrades, collateral haircuts, and transfer restrictions across currencies and time horizons; results inform funding plans. The Parent Company and IHC provide funding, while liquidity is maintained across entities to meet tolerances and requirements during disruption.

nodes.title: Contingency funding plan

Contingency funding plan

The CFP also identifies the alternative contingent funding and liquidity resources available to the Firm and its legal entities in a period of stress.

nodes.title: LCR and HQLA
nodes.summary: The LCR rule requires the Firm and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to maintain eligible, unencumbered high-quality liquid assets (mainly cash and liquid securities) sufficient to cover estimated net cash outflows during 30 days of stress, with a minimum LCR of 100%. Excess bank HQLA unavailable to non-bank affiliates is excluded from the Firm’s reported total. Average LCR data for three months ended December 2024, September 2024, and December 2023 show Firm LCRs of 113%, 114%, and 113%, and bank LCRs of 124%, 121%, and 129%, alongside HQLA, outflow, and net excess amounts. Notes describe cash and securities composition, valuation, and exclusions. The bank’s quarter-over-quarter LCR increase reflected CIB Markets activity, partly offset by lower securities values and maturities; its year-over-year decline reflected dividends and lending, partly offset by securities values, reduced unencumbered non-HQLA AFS securities, CIB Markets activity, and debt issuance. LCRs fluctuate with business activity, Federal Reserve actions, HQLA, and outflows; further detail is available in the Firm’s U.S. LCR disclosures.

nodes.title: Liquidity sources

Their fair value fell from $649 billion in 2023 to $594 billion in 2024, mainly due to reductions in Treasury and CIO AFS securities, excess bank HQLA, and CIB trading assets; liquidity raised depends on market conditions. Available cash and securities totaled about $1.4 trillion in both years, comprising eligible HQLA of $798 billion and $834 billion, respectively, plus those securities. Collateral-supported FHLB and Federal Reserve discount-window borrowing capacity rose from $340 billion to $413 billion, chiefly because more commercial loans and credit card receivables were pledged. This excludes cash and securities already counted elsewhere or pledged to central banks, and the Firm does not consider central-bank borrowing a primary liquidity source.

nodes.title: NSFR

For the three months ended December 31, 2024, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. met the 100% minimum, based on the Firm’s interpretation of the final rule. Further information is available in the Firm’s U.S. NSFR Disclosure report.

nodes.title: Reputation Risk Management
nodes.summary: Reputation risk is the possibility that actions or inaction damage stakeholders’ perceptions of the Firm’s integrity or competence, potentially causing financial, legal, regulatory, or other harm. Risks can arise from employees, business activities and strategies, or clients, customers, and counterparties. An independent function sets Firmwide governance and standards and oversees processes and infrastructure for consistent identification, escalation, and monitoring. Each business, Corporate, and employee must consider reputational effects when evaluating products, transactions, relationships, jurisdictions, processes, and other activities; environmental impacts and social concerns are also relevant.

Explains how the Firm identifies, governs, monitors, and manages strategic, capital, liquidity, and reputation risks. Covers leadership and Board oversight; strategic planning aligned with risk appetite, budgets, capital, earnings, and balance-sheet objectives; capital governance, allocation, regulatory requirements, stress tests, distributions, and contingency actions; liquidity limits, funding, stress scenarios, regulatory ratios, resources, and ratings; and reputation-risk sources, impacts, firmwide standards, escalation, and responsibilities, including environmental and social considerations.

Credit and Investment Risk Management

nodes.title: Stress testing

Stress tests apply centrally defined economic scenarios, assess migration, delinquency, and losses, incorporate additional industry or country stresses, and inform risk appetite and counterparty decisions.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and management
nodes.summary: The Firm’s credit-risk framework safeguards independent, accurate approval and active monitoring at transaction and portfolio levels through approval authorities, concentration limits, risk-rating methods, reviews, distressed-exposure guidance, and independent validation of models and assumptions. Consumer risk monitoring tracks delinquencies, concentrations, economic trends, forecasts, and industry benchmarks to inform underwriting and loss estimates. Wholesale risk is monitored by portfolio, industry, client, and counterparty, with periodically reviewed limits and stress-based loss constraints; exposure is managed through underwriting, syndication, sales, securitization, derivatives, netting, and collateral. Independent Credit Review assesses wholesale risk grades and their timeliness, and evaluates credit-management analysis, monitoring, LGD rationale, and policy compliance. Note 12 discusses consumer and wholesale loans.

nodes.title: Risk reporting

Detailed portfolio reports cover industries, clients, counterparties, customers, products, and geographies; senior management reviews the adequacy of credit-loss allowances at least quarterly. Risk trends and limit exceptions are regularly shared with and discussed by risk committees, senior management, and the Board.
