Residential real estate and auto/other repayment estimates use weighted-average loan balances and rates by remaining term; credit card loans are also included. Amounts are in millions, with notes that within-one-year totals include loans held for sale and at fair value, and auto/other loans include overdrafts. It references Note 12 for loan-class details.

nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards declined from year-end 2023, mainly due to residential real estate and scored auto loans. Residential mortgage discussion covers portfolio composition and changes in retained, held-for-sale, fair-value, and nonaccrual loans; interest-only mortgages and HELOC balances and risk management; government-guaranteed loan delinquencies; geographic concentration and improved estimated LTVs. Auto and other loans declined mainly from securitizations, while charge-offs rose with weaker used-car values. Tables report nonperforming assets and nonaccrual-loan activity for 2024 and 2023, with exclusions for government-insured past-due mortgages; Note 12 is cited for further credit-quality details.

nodes.title: Credit Card
key_items: Geographic and FICO composition of credit card loans
nodes.summary: Credit card loans grew in 2024 due to new accounts and revolving balances; delinquency rates rose slightly as expected, and net charge-offs increased from vintage seasoning, credit normalization, and balance growth. Cards generally remain on accrual until charged off, while the allowance covers estimated uncollectible accrued and billed interest and fees. Five states held 47% of retained balances, up from 46%; Note 12 provides portfolio details. Wholesale credit risk arises across client, counterparty, lending, trading, operating, and financing activities; the portfolio is actively managed, with loans also distributed to manage risk. In 2024, wholesale loans rose $19.8 billion, commitments fell $5.3 billion, and nonperforming exposure increased $2.3 billion, largely due to real estate downgrades. Net charge-offs were $822 million, mainly from office real estate and client-specific losses. The table presents 2024 and 2023 wholesale portfolio assets, commitments, credit exposure, nonperforming amounts, and credit-risk management offsets, with notes explaining customer receivables and credit derivatives.

Describes the Firm’s primarily prime retained consumer portfolio, its products and mortgage disposition practices, and presents 2024–2023 exposure, nonaccrual, charge-off, recovery, and loan maturity data with definitions and exclusions. Reviews consumer loans excluding credit cards, including mortgage and auto portfolio changes, risk factors, geographic and loan-to-value trends, and nonperforming activity. Covers credit-card growth, delinquencies, charge-offs, accrual and allowance policies, and geographic concentration. Also summarizes wholesale credit risk management and changes in loans, commitments, nonperforming exposure, charge-offs, and risk offsets.

nodes.title: Wholesale Credit Portfolio
Wholesale credit portfolio
nodes.summary: The Firm’s wholesale credit risk arises from client and counterparty underwriting, lending, trading, hedging, operating and securities-financing activities, and cash placed with banks. It retains some loans and syndicates others, while actively reviewing credit quality, transaction structure, collateral and concentrations. The portfolio covers CIB, AWM, Corporate and certain risk-rated CCB exposures. In 2024, loans rose $19.8 billion, commitments fell $5.3 billion, and nonperforming exposure increased $2.3 billion, mainly from downgraded real estate exposures. Net charge-offs were $822 million, driven largely by real estate and client-specific losses. The table presents 2024 and 2023 portfolio assets, commitments, credit-management derivatives and collateral, credit exposure, and nonperforming amounts; notes explain customer receivables and credit-risk-management instruments.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – maturity and ratings profile
nodes.summary: Presents wholesale credit portfolio maturity and internal-rating profiles at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including retained loans, derivative receivables and collateral, lending commitments, loans held for sale or at fair value, customer receivables, total exposure, and credit-risk-management derivatives/notes. It defines investment grade as generally BBB-/Baa3-equivalent or higher and notes collateral and structural support inform ratings. Tables show maturity buckets, investment- versus noninvestment-grade amounts, and investment-grade percentages. Footnotes explain loan sources, derivative accounting and rating basis, purchased protection and credit-related notes, and maturity methodology.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industry exposures
nodes.summary: The Firm manages and diversifies industry credit exposures, with attention to industries with actual or potential credit concerns. Criticized exposures follow U.S. banking regulator categories: special mention, substandard and doubtful. Excluding loans held for sale and at fair value, criticized exposure was $44.7 billion (3.5% of wholesale exposure) in 2024, versus $41.4 billion (3.3%) in 2023; $39.9 billion of the 2024 total was performing. The increase reflected Real Estate downgrades, mainly Multifamily and Office, and new Technology and Media commitments, partly offset by Consumer & Retail portfolio activity and upgrades. The accompanying table presents exposures by industry for both years; industry classification is generally based on the client’s or counterparty’s primary business, with further concentration details in Note 4.

nodes.title: Wholesale credit exposure – industries (a)
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents JPMorgan Chase’s 2024 and 2023 wholesale credit exposure by industry, including investment-grade and criticized exposures, past-due loans, charge-offs/recoveries, collateral, and credit protection, with definitions and exclusions in footnotes. It explains industry classification and selected state/municipal securities, cash exclusions, and exposure scope. Real estate detail compares 2024 with 2023 by property type, credit exposure, investment-grade share, and drawn percentage; criticized real estate exposure rose $3.2 billion, mainly from Multifamily and Office downgrades. Notes describe multifamily performance and California concentration, diversified property types, and real estate collateral and unsecured exposures.

nodes.title: Real Estate
nodes.summary: The discussion reports JPMorgan’s 2024 credit exposures and criticized-exposure trends for Real Estate, Consumer & Retail, and Oil & Gas, with 2023 comparisons. Tables break exposures down by industry subsector and show loans and lending-related commitments, derivative receivables, total credit exposure, investment-grade percentages, and drawn percentages. Real Estate exposure was $207.1 billion; criticized exposure rose $3.2 billion, mainly from Multifamily and Office downgrades. Consumer & Retail exposure was $129.8 billion; criticized exposure fell $1.4 billion through portfolio activity and upgrades, partly offset by downgrades. Oil & Gas exposure was $31.7 billion; criticized exposure increased from $123 million to $192 million. Notes describe subsector definitions, collateralization, investment-grade status, geographic concentration, and table metrics.

nodes.title: Consumer & Retail
nodes.summary: The text reports December 31, 2024 Consumer & Retail exposure of $129.8 billion, down from $127.1 billion in 2023, with criticized exposure falling $1.4 billion to $6.9 billion due to portfolio activity and upgrades, partly offset by downgrades. It provides 2024 and 2023 exposure by subsector, investment-grade percentages, and drawn ratios, plus notes on retail and leisure categories, collateralization, and unsecured credit quality. Oil & Gas exposure was $31.7 billion versus $34.5 billion in 2023; criticized exposure rose from $123 million to $192 million. Subsector exposure, investment-grade and drawn ratios, business definitions, collateralization, reserve-based lending, and unsecured credit quality are also detailed.

nodes.title: Oil & Gas
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports 2024 and 2023 credit exposure by sub-sector for Consumer & Retail and Oil & Gas, including loans and lending commitments, derivative receivables, credit exposure, investment-grade and drawn percentages, and changes in criticized exposure. It notes portfolio collateral and sub-sector definitions. It also describes wholesale lending and directs readers to Note 12 for loan credit-quality details, then presents 2024–2023 nonaccrual-loan activity and wholesale net charge-offs, recoveries, average retained loans, and charge-off rates.

nodes.title: Loans and Wholesale Nonaccrual Activity
nodes.summary: The Firm’s wholesale businesses lend to corporate, institutional, and high-net-worth clients; Note 12 discusses delinquencies, modifications, and other credit indicators. Nonaccrual exposure rose $2.2 billion in 2024, mainly from downgrades in Office, Healthcare, and Consumer & Retail real estate. A table compares 2024 and 2023 beginning balances, additions, reductions by category, net changes, and ending balances. The page also introduces net charge-offs/recoveries, excluding gains or losses on nonaccrual loan sales recorded in noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Wholesale net charge-offs/(recoveries)
nodes.summary: Wholesale net charge-offs and recoveries for 2024 and 2023: average loans retained were $673,310 million and $646,875 million, gross charge-offs were $1,022 million and $1,011 million, and gross recoveries collected were $200 million and $132 million. Net charge-offs were $822 million and $879 million, with net charge-off rates of 0.12% and 0.14%, respectively.

nodes.title: Maturities and sensitivity to changes in interest rates
nodes.summary: The text reports wholesale loan maturities and fixed- versus variable-rate distributions at December 31, 2024, with footnotes on reset-rate loans and loans due within one year, and presents 2024–2023 net charge-offs or recoveries, average retained loans, and loss rates by loan class. It explains that contractual wholesale lending commitments and guarantees are maximum potential exposures but generally do not indicate expected exposure or funding needs. Customer margin receivables are collateralized and actively monitored, so typically require no credit-loss allowance. It describes derivative uses and counterparty risks, mitigation through netting and collateral, collateral coverage rates, derivative receivable fair values and their increase, and additional collateral that supports exposure but is excluded from reported receivables.

nodes.title: Lending Commitments and Customer Receivables
nodes.summary: The Firm uses commitments and guarantees to meet clients’ financing needs; their contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but generally do not reflect expected exposure or funding needs because they are often unused, refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expired. Customer receivables are collateralized brokerage margin loans, managed through margin requirements and ongoing monitoring. Short-term maturities, collateral, and rights to demand additional margin generally mitigate losses, so allowances are usually unnecessary; when required, expected losses are estimated using collateral value and default probability. Receivables are reported in accrued interest and accounts receivable.

nodes.title: Derivative contracts
nodes.summary: The text explains how JPMorgan Chase uses derivatives to meet clients’ risk-management needs, make markets and manage its own risks, and describes counterparty/CCP credit exposure and mitigation through netting and collateral. It reports collateral coverage and 2024–2023 derivative receivables, collateral deductions and investment-grade ratings shares. It defines Peak, DRE and AVG exposure measures, their uses, CVA and wrong-way risk management, and hedging of CVA. A graph shows projected exposure over ten years, generally declining after year one if no new trades are added.

nodes.title: Derivative Receivables and Credit Exposure
nodes.summary: Tables report net derivative receivables after cash, liquid securities and other collateral, and investment-grade versus noninvestment-grade exposure for 2024 and 2023. The text explains Peak, DRE and AVG measures of potential credit loss, their uses in limits, reporting, pricing, capital and CVA, and how CVA reflects counterparty credit quality. It describes active risk management, wrong-way risk and possible CVA adjustments, hedging CVA changes with derivatives, and portfolio exposure profiles showing generally declining exposure after year one if no trades are added.

nodes.title: Exposure profile of derivatives measures
nodes.summary: The text presents a derivatives exposure profile chart as of December 31, 2024, and explains JPMorgan Chase’s use of credit derivatives as a market-maker and to manage its own credit risk. Credit portfolio management derivatives protect against risks from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale derivatives counterparties; other end-user derivatives cover certain securities and are excluded from that category. Net protection used for portfolio management totaled $40.888 billion in 2024 versus $36.989 billion in 2023. These derivatives are fair-valued without hedge accounting, while related loans are accrued, creating potentially unrepresentative earnings volatility. CDS hedge effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, contract terms, and maturities; the Firm seeks maturity alignment and monitors remaining differences.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
nodes.summary:
Management’s discussion and analysis
Credit derivatives
The Firm uses credit derivatives for two primary purposes: first, in its capacity as a market-maker, and second, as an end-user to manage the Firm’s own credit risk associated with various exposures.

nodes.title: Credit portfolio management activities
nodes.summary: The Firm uses credit derivatives to mitigate credit risk from loans, lending commitments, and wholesale-business derivative counterparty exposures; other derivatives used for market-making securities exposures are excluded. Net protection used for portfolio management totaled $40.9 billion in 2024 versus $37.0 billion in 2023, covering loans and commitments and derivative receivables. These derivatives do not qualify for hedge accounting and are fair-valued through principal transactions revenue, while related lending exposures use accrual accounting, creating earnings volatility that may not reflect overall credit-value changes. CDS hedging effectiveness can differ due to reference entities, credit-event terms, or maturities; the Firm generally aligns protection maturities with exposures and monitors differences.

Covers the wholesale credit portfolio’s sources, scope, management and 2024–2023 trends in loans, commitments, nonperforming and criticized exposures, charge-offs and recoveries. Tables detail exposure by maturity, internal credit rating, industry and subsector—including Real Estate, Consumer & Retail, and Oil & Gas—with collateral, investment-grade status, drawn amounts, past dues and credit protection. The section also discusses nonaccrual activity, loan maturities and interest-rate sensitivity, lending commitments and customer margin receivables, derivative counterparty exposure and mitigation, exposure measures and profiles, and credit derivatives used for portfolio protection, including hedging limitations and accounting-driven earnings volatility.

nodes.title: Allowance for Credit Losses
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
Allocation of allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The text explains JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses, its components and balance-sheet presentation, and the 2024 increase to $26.9 billion, including consumer and wholesale drivers. It describes the five-scenario macroeconomic estimate, adverse-case unemployment and GDP outcomes, central-case forecasts for 2024 and 2023, and references for further information. Tables detail 2024 and 2023 allowance movements, charge-offs, provisions, ending balances, impairment methods, retained loans and credit ratios, plus the allowance allocation by loan class and its share of retained loans.

nodes.title: Investment Portfolio Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s investment portfolio and market risk management. Investment risk involves principal loss or reduced returns; securities are mainly high-quality Treasury/CIO holdings, while principal investments are largely private, long-term holdings managed by business units. It reports 2024 securities carrying value and average rating, and principal investment carrying values for 2024 and 2023, including tax-oriented and private equity/debt/real-asset investments and an accounting-guidance update. Governance includes risk committees, independent valuation controls, approved limits, and stress testing. Market Risk Management oversees firmwide market risk, policies, measurement, limits, and stress assessments, using VaR, stress tests, drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, economic-value sensitivity, and other metrics. Limits reflect market and business conditions; exposures and breaches are monitored, reported, escalated, and remediated or temporarily accommodated. The text also notes model limitations and periodic metric review.

Defines credit, investment and market risk, the Firm’s exposures, governance, measurement, monitoring, stress testing, reporting and capital and loss-allowance practices. Covers consumer and wholesale portfolios, including exposures, credit quality, concentrations, nonperforming loans, delinquencies, charge-offs, recoveries, commitments, collateral, derivatives, ratings, maturities and risk mitigation; details credit-loss allowance methods, forecasts and trends; and describes investment holdings, valuation controls, market-risk metrics, limits, escalation and model limitations.

nodes.title: Market Risk Management
Market Risk Management and Measurement
key_items: Measures used to capture market risk
nodes.summary: Market risk arises when changes in interest or foreign exchange rates, equity or commodity prices, credit spreads, or implied volatilities affect asset and liability values. Market Risk Management monitors firmwide risk, establishes policies and procedures, supports risk-return decisions, reduces performance volatility, and informs senior management, the Board, and regulators. Its responsibilities include maintaining policy frameworks; independently measuring and monitoring risk; setting and overseeing limits; and conducting stress tests and qualitative assessments. Risk is assessed using multiple statistical and nonstatistical measures: value-at-risk, stress testing, profit-and-loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, economic value sensitivity, and other sensitivity measures.

nodes.title: Risk monitoring and control
nodes.summary: JPMorgan Chase manages market risk through volatility-, liquidity-, client-activity- and strategy-sensitive limits at firm, business and legal-entity levels, including VaR, stress and other measures. Limits are reviewed, approved, monitored and escalated; breaches prompt corrective action or temporary increases. The text outlines each business’s activities, market risks, positions and measures, and notes model uncertainty and periodic enhancement. It explains Risk Management VaR’s historical-simulation framework, assumptions, uses and limitations, proxies and complementary stress testing, and the distinct ten-day, 99%-confidence Regulatory VaR used for capital requirements.

nodes.title: VaR
Value-at-risk
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes its historical-simulation VaR framework, based on the prior 12 months, used for daily risk management and regulatory capital measurement. Risk Management VaR uses a one-day horizon and approximately 95% confidence; Regulatory VaR uses a ten-day horizon and approximately 99%, with different covered positions and diversification treatment. The text explains model inputs, aggregation, limitations, proxies for illiquid products, complementary stress measures, data differences, and periodic model updates. It presents 2024 and 2023 VaR averages, minimums and maximums by business and risk type, defines diversification and scope footnotes, and notes average total VaR rose $4 million in 2024, mainly due to Visa C shares and credit protection, partly offset by fixed-income volatility rolling out. A quarterly chart shows VaR’s second-quarter rise and decline, largely reflecting Visa C exposure.

nodes.title: Total VaR
nodes.summary: The text presents the Firm’s 95% confidence-level VaR results for 2024 and 2023, including average, minimum and maximum VaR by CIB risk type, Credit Portfolio, business segment, Corporate, Other, and diversification effects. It explains that VaR varies with positions, volatility and diversification, defines diversification benefits, and provides notes on segment reorganization, CVA and credit-protection treatment, AWM presentation, and legacy equity holdings. Average Total VaR rose $4 million in 2024, mainly due to Visa C shares and purchased credit protection, partly offset by fixed-income volatility rolling out of the look-back period. A quarterly graph’s second-quarter rise and decline primarily reflected changing Visa C exposure.

nodes.title: Daily Risk Management VaR
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan’s daily Risk Management VaR backtesting: daily backtesting gains and losses are compared with prior-day VaR, exclude several revenue components, and follow Basel III definitions. Exceptions occur when losses exceed VaR; five per 100 trading days are statistically expected, though volatility differences can change observed counts. In 2024, the Firm had gains on 179 of 260 days and eight exceptions, including three in Q4. Firmwide loss days may differ from CIB Markets loss days because positions and included revenue differ. A chart groups daily losses as percentages of VaR in 50-point intervals, showing exceptions above 100%; results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory VaR backtesting.

nodes.title: Distribution of Daily Backtesting Gains and Losses
nodes.summary: The text describes JPMorgan Chase’s stress-testing framework, which supplements VaR by assessing hypothetical simultaneous market shocks across asset classes, regions, and risk factors. Scenarios cover rallies, sell-offs, tail and idiosyncratic events, and basis risk; results inform limits, management and Board reporting, CCAR, and risk appetite. Methodologies and models are governed and reviewed by risk committees. Profit-and-loss drawdowns track declines from year-to-date revenue peaks. Structural interest rate risk arises from trading and banking activities; CTC governance, Treasury and CIO, and independent risk oversight set policy, monitor limits, and manage exposure, generally through securities and derivatives. Key drivers include repricing and maturity mismatches, yield-curve changes, and changing maturities; business units transfer manageable exposure to Treasury and CIO through funds transfer pricing.

Explains JPMorganChase’s historical-simulation VaR framework, including horizons, confidence levels, covered positions, aggregation, diversification, limitations, proxies, stress measures, data and model updates. Reports 2024 and 2023 VaR averages, ranges and quarterly trends by risk type and business, with scope and methodology notes; average total VaR increased $4 million in 2024, mainly from Visa C shares and credit protection. Describes daily backtesting, expected and observed exceptions, loss distributions, and differences from regulatory backtesting. Also covers stress testing scenarios, governance and uses, P&L drawdowns, and structural interest-rate risk oversight, drivers and transfer of exposures to Treasury and CIO.

nodes.title: Earnings-at-risk
key_items: Other risk measures Stress testing; Profit and loss drawdowns; Structural interest rate risk management
Key risk drivers and risk management process
nodes.summary: The text describes stress testing as a complement to VaR, including scenario design, governance, reporting, CCAR use, and risk-appetite oversight; it also defines profit-and-loss drawdowns. It explains structural interest-rate risk, its governance, drivers, transfer to Treasury and CIO, and management through securities and derivatives. It details earnings-at-risk scenarios, assumptions, sensitivities, 2024 assumption and balance-sheet changes, and limitations. Finally, it outlines Economic Value Sensitivity, its balance-sheet scope, key assumptions, limits, and differences from fair-value measurements.

nodes.title: Non-U.S. Dollar FX Risk
nodes.summary: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk arises when exchange-rate changes affect the Firm’s assets, liabilities, or future results. Structural exposures come from capital investments, forecast expenses and revenue, investment securities, and foreign-currency debt. Treasury and CIO, in partnership with the LOBs, primarily manage these risks and may use derivatives to hedge them. Further information is referenced in Business Segment & Corporate Results, page 71.

nodes.title: Other sensitivity-based measures
key_items: Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk; Activity
nodes.summary: The text reports sensitivity-based market-risk impacts on net revenue, OCI, and noninterest expense for debt/equity and credit/funding exposures outside VaR and earnings-at-risk, including measures, 2024/2023 results, hedging treatment, caveats, and footnote classifications/exclusions. It then describes country-risk oversight, responsibilities, exposure sources and country attribution, aggregation and exclusions, measurement methods for deposits, lending, securities financing, securities, derivatives and credit derivatives, assumptions that may affect reported exposure, and differences from FFIEC reporting.

Explains how JPMorgan Chase identifies, measures, monitors, and controls market risk from rates, currencies, prices, spreads, and volatility. Covers governance, policies, limits, escalation, business exposures, model uncertainty, VaR methods and results, backtesting, stress testing, drawdowns, structural interest-rate risk, earnings-at-risk, and economic value sensitivity, including assumptions and limitations. Also addresses non-U.S. dollar FX hedging, sensitivity-based impacts on revenue, OCI, and expenses, and country-risk oversight, exposure measurement, attribution, exclusions, and reporting differences.

nodes.title: Country Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text outlines JPMorgan Chase’s country-risk framework: independent governance, policies, sovereign ratings, limits, monitoring, early-warning tools and scenario analysis. It explains exposure attribution and measurement across deposits, lending, securities, financing and derivatives, noting exclusions, assumptions and differences from FFIEC reporting. Stress tests assess country-crisis losses, while regular reporting tracks exposure, limits and trends. It presents the top 20 non-U.S. country exposures for 2024 versus 2023, explains Germany’s and Japan’s increases, and notes Russia exposure is considered immaterial; table definitions and coverage are provided.

nodes.title: Climate Risk Management
nodes.summary: Climate risk is defined as climate-change threats to the Firm and its clients, operations and strategy, categorized as acute or chronic physical risks and risks from the transition to a lower-carbon economy. A dedicated function maintains firmwide climate strategy, policies, metrics, scenarios, stress tests and data infrastructure; business units manage risks and comply with applicable laws. Climate risk is integrated into governance, with significant matters escalated to risk committees and the Board Risk Committee. Operational risk covers adverse outcomes from failed processes or systems, people or external events, including compliance, conduct, legal, estimation and model risks. The CCOR framework governs identification, measurement, monitoring, testing, management and reporting. Business units manage risks, supported by control managers; independent CCOR leadership sets standards and reports to the Board Risk Committee. Self-assessments and independent reviews identify control gaps and emerging risks. Measurement includes control assessments, capital and loss estimates using the LDA model, AMA inputs, scenario analysis and stressed conditions; insurance is excluded from AMA capital estimates. Stress testing supports CCAR, and monitoring and testing assess business-unit compliance.

nodes.title: Operational Risk Management
Operational Risk Management Framework
key_items: Operational Risk Governance; Operational Risk Identification; Operational Risk Measurement
Management of Operational Risk; Operational Risk Reporting
nodes.summary: Operational risk arises from failed processes or systems, human factors, or external events and includes compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risks, such as fraud, disruptions, cyberattacks, misconduct, regulatory failures, and vendor failures. The CCOR framework governs, identifies, measures, monitors, tests, manages, and reports risk. LOBs and Corporate own risk management; control managers execute the framework, while independent CCOR leadership sets standards under Board oversight. Identification uses self-assessments and independent challenge. Measurement includes control reviews, capital and loss estimates using LDA and AMA, scenario analysis, and stress testing; insurance is excluded from AMA capital. Independent monitoring tests controls and compliance. Issues are escalated and remediated through action plans. Firmwide reporting tracks indicators and risk appetite, with escalation to senior management and the Board.

nodes.title: Insurance
nodes.summary:
Insurance
One of the ways in which operational risk may be mitigated is through insurance maintained by the Firm. The Firm purchases insurance from commercial insurers and maintains a wholly-owned captive insurer, Park Assurance Company. Insurance may also be required by third parties with whom the Firm does business.

nodes.title: Subcategories and examples of operational risks
key_items: Firmwide resiliency risk; Payment fraud risk
nodes.summary: Operational risks include compliance, conduct, legal, and estimation/model risks, with further examples covering resiliency, payment fraud, outsourcing, and cybersecurity. The Firm’s resiliency framework prepares for, withstands, and recovers from disruptions through governance, training, planning, testing, and coordination with related risk programs. Payment-fraud controls are supplemented by employee and client education; third-party oversight frameworks manage supplier and affiliate relationships and mitigate performance, data-loss, and disruption risks. Cybersecurity threats are evolving and may originate from the Firm, third parties, or clients; controls, monitoring, and external engagement address them, though material future harm remains possible. The CISO leads the Information Security Program and functions covering cyber operations, technology governance and controls, awareness training, privacy, and technology recovery. Incident response includes recovery and coordination with authorities. Governance integrates cybersecurity into operational risk management, with independent challenge, management committees, and periodic Board, Audit Committee, and Risk Committee oversight.

nodes.title: Compliance Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text defines compliance risk and conduct risk as operational-risk subcategories and describes their scope, governance, and management. Business lines and Corporate own and manage these risks, while Operational Risk and Compliance independently oversees compliance, sets policies and standards, and reports significant issues to board committees. Compliance covers legal and regulatory obligations across products, jurisdictions, client interactions, employee activities, and fiduciary duties, with other functions overseeing specialized obligations. The Code of Conduct sets integrity and ethical expectations, requires reporting violations, provides employee training and annual affirmations, and offers a global, anonymous-where-legal hotline with anti-retaliation protections; the Audit Committee receives periodic updates. Conduct-risk management follows the same oversight structure and includes employee-life-cycle practices, periodic assessments, metrics and issue reviews, and education.

nodes.title: Conduct Risk Management
nodes.summary: Conduct risk is operational risk arising from employee actions or misconduct that may cause unfair customer outcomes, undermine market integrity, harm employees or the Firm, or damage its reputation. Each line of business and Corporate function manages its risk in line with the Firm’s Business Principles and Code, which guide expected conduct and ethical, legally compliant business practices. Oversight is coordinated like Compliance risk. Management spans the employee lifecycle, including hiring, training, performance, promotion, and compensation; relevant groups periodically assess risk, review metrics and issues, and provide education as appropriate.

nodes.title: Legal Risk Management
nodes.summary: Legal risk is operational risk arising from actual or alleged failure to meet obligations under applicable law, agreements, or the Firm’s products and services. The global Legal function manages litigation, enforcement, investigations, contracts, products, disclosures, new initiatives, disputes, legal interpretation and advocacy, and advises business units, Corporate, and the Board. It manages outside counsel and advises the Conflicts Office on potentially conflicted wholesale transactions. The General Counsel reports to the CEO and serves on key risk and control committees; Legal reports significant matters to the Board and Audit Committee, advises committees and business units, and addresses potential reputation risks.

nodes.title: Estimations and Model Risk Management
nodes.summary: Model risk is the operational risk of adverse decisions from incorrect or misused estimates. The Firm uses models and analytical or judgment-based estimates—including AI and machine learning—for valuation, risk, capital, stress testing, credit-loss allowances, and business decisions. Independent MRGR governs relevant policies and reviews models; business users and developers own, develop, test, maintain, and monitor them. Models are tiered by complexity, exposure, and reliance, and MRGR assesses suitability, methods, assumptions, and testing. New models and material changes generally need prior approval; limited exceptions may require interim mitigations. Uncertainty can rise when market, economic, or acquired-asset conditions differ from model-development data, requiring greater judgment. The text also refers readers to the Firm’s critical accounting estimates and Note 2 for valuation methods.

Covers the Firm’s operational risk framework: risk ownership, independent oversight, identification, measurement, testing, remediation, escalation, and reporting. Describes insurance as a mitigation and examples including resiliency, payment fraud, outsourcing, and cybersecurity. Explains compliance and conduct governance, ethical standards, employee training and reporting, and lifecycle risk management; Legal’s role in legal obligations and disputes; and model and estimation risk governance, validation, approvals, uncertainty, and uses including AI and machine learning.

Describes JPMorganChase’s firmwide risk framework, accountability, three lines of defense, risk appetite, and Board and management oversight. Covers governance committees and functions, then explains how strategic, capital, liquidity, reputation, credit, investment, market, country, climate, operational, compliance, conduct, legal, and model-estimation risks are identified, measured, monitored, controlled, stress-tested, escalated, and reported. Includes portfolio exposures and loss allowances, market-risk metrics and sensitivities, country exposures, climate scenarios, operational controls and remediation, and mitigation through insurance.

nodes.title: Critical Accounting Estimates Used by the Firm
Allowance for credit losses
key_items: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES USED BY THE FIRM
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes controls and governance for critical accounting estimates, emphasizing consistent, independently reviewed methods and management judgment. Its credit-loss allowance covers retained loans, lending commitments and investment securities, and depends on forecasts, historical losses, risk assessments, collateral and expected asset life. Eight-quarter forecasts use hundreds of macroeconomic variables, with key drivers varying by portfolio; acquired First Republic exposures entered the wholesale model in Q2 2024. A comparison of central and adverse scenarios shows modeled increases of about $850 million for residential real estate, $3.7 billion for cards and $4.1 billion for wholesale exposures, but is not a prediction of total allowance changes because of scenario weighting, nonlinear and interrelated factors, portfolio and borrower changes, and qualitative adjustments. Management considers its 2024 estimates reasonable despite forecast uncertainty.

nodes.title: Fair value
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase measures many assets and liabilities at fair value on a recurring basis, including derivatives, structured notes and some securities-financing agreements; certain collateral-backed loans are measured nonrecurringly. The table reports 2024 fair-value assets by category, recurring versus nonrecurring measurement, Level 3 balances and their share of total Firm assets, with a note on derivative netting. Valuation requires judgment, especially for Level 3 instruments with significant unobservable inputs. Management selects models, assesses market and empirical inputs, and applies adjustments for credit, funding, liquidity and portfolio risks. Uncertainty, volatility and methodological choices can affect estimates and reported gains or losses; further details are in Note 2.

nodes.title: Goodwill impairment
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP requires goodwill to be assigned to reporting units and tested for impairment at least annually; the Firm’s methodology is described in Note 15. Management exercises significant judgment and assigns acquisition goodwill to related units. For 2024, it reviewed economic conditions, equity costs, actual results, and forecasts, concluding goodwill was not impaired: each unit’s fair value exceeded carrying value by at least 10%, with no significant impairment risk indicated. Forecasts reflect short-term business outlook and long-term growth and return assumptions, benchmarked against third-party and peer data where possible. Note 15 provides further details.

nodes.title: Credit card rewards liability
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase credit cardholders earn generally unlimited, non-expiring points redeemable for cash or account credits, gift cards, and travel. The firm accrues an estimated liability as rewards are earned and reduces it upon redemption. It was $14.4 billion at year-end 2024, up from $13.2 billion in 2023, as points earned from higher spending and promotions outpaced redemptions; it is reported in accounts payable and other liabilities. The estimate depends on redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions, reviewed using historical results, customer behavior, and management judgment. A 25-basis-point increase in redemption rate combined with a 1-basis-point increase in cost per point would raise the 2024 liability by about $442 million.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s income tax accounting involves interpreting complex U.S. and foreign tax laws, estimating tax liabilities and uncertain positions, and resolving disputes through audits, appeals, or courts; revisions may materially affect results. Deferred taxes reflect differences between financial and tax reporting, use enacted rates, and recognize assets when realization is more likely than not. The Firm reviews NOL and foreign tax credit carryforwards, future taxable income, and tax strategies, applying or reversing valuation allowances as appropriate; at December 31, 2024, deferred tax assets were considered realizable net of the allowance. Uncertain tax benefits are reassessed as information changes and measured at the largest benefit more likely than not to be realized; final outcomes may affect tax expense and effective rates. Current and deferred provisions rely on estimates, with return-related adjustments recorded when filings and global implications are known.

Listed risks include economic, geopolitical, regulatory, market, credit, operational, technology, cyber, climate, reputation, staffing, competition, controls and other factors. nodes.title: Offsetting assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: U.S. GAAP allows net presentation of certain derivative, collateral, repurchase, and securities-lending balances when legal and other conditions are met; the Firm elects this treatment where eligible. Master netting agreements reduce counterparty risk by enabling transactions and collateral to be terminated, valued, offset, and settled through a single payment, with collateral agreements covering margin, set-off, and liquidation rights. Cash-flow statements define cash as cash and due from banks and deposits with banks. A 2024 proportional-amortization standard for eligible tax-credit investments changed the classification and timing of certain alternative-energy investment amortization, reduced retained earnings by $161 million, and increased first-quarter tax expense by about $450 million and the effective tax rate by two percentage points, with no material net-income effect; it also adds disclosure and reassessment requirements. A 2023 fair-value-hedging standard expanded portfolio-layer hedging; the Firm transferred and designated certain held-to-maturity securities as available-for-sale, with no material retained-earnings impact.

nodes.title: Netting, Cash Flows, and Tax Investment Accounting

nodes.title: Note 2 - Fair value measurement
Valuation process
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase measures certain assets, liabilities, and lending commitments at fair value on a recurring or, in specific circumstances such as impairment, nonrecurring basis. Fair value uses market prices or valuation models with observable and unobservable inputs, and may include adjustments; estimates depend on judgment and can differ from other participants’ valuations. Risk functions estimate values, while independent Finance valuation control verifies them and sets adjustments, overseen by senior risk and finance governance forums. Verification uses independent data and additional analyses and reviews for less observable or complex positions. Adjustments may address liquidity, large net open risk positions, uncertainty in unobservable inputs, counterparty and own credit, and funding; Level 1 quoted prices are not adjusted.

nodes.title: Valuation model review and approval
nodes.summary: When market prices or comparable quotes are unavailable, fair value is generally estimated with models using transaction terms and market-based or independently sourced inputs; those inputs undergo the stated price-verification process. Under Firm policy, MRGR reviews and approves new models and material changes before operational use. Exceptions may allow interim use before approval, potentially subject to MRGR-required risk mitigations such as restricting trading.

nodes.title: Fair value hierarchy
nodes.summary: Defines the U.S. GAAP fair value hierarchy: Level 1 uses unadjusted quoted prices for identical instruments in active markets; Level 2 uses observable inputs; Level 3 includes significant unobservable inputs. Classification follows the lowest significant input level. It outlines JPMorgan’s valuation methods and typical hierarchy levels for securities financing, wholesale and consumer loans, securities, commodities, derivatives, mortgage servicing rights, private equity, fund investments, VIE interests, and structured notes. Methods include quoted or comparable prices, broker quotes, discounted cash flows, NAV, models and product-specific market, credit, collateral, cash-flow, and risk inputs; adjustments include counterparty, funding, and own-credit risk. It introduces tables of fair-value assets and liabilities by product and hierarchy for 2024 and 2023.

nodes.title: Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis

The text also describes Level 3 valuation processes, judgment and inputs, the scope and interpretation of disclosed input ranges and averages, and risk management of observable components.

nodes.title: Fair value measurements using significant unobservable inputs
Level 3 valuations
nodes.summary: The text explains the Firm’s Level 3 fair-value process: management selects valuation techniques and uses judgment to estimate significant unobservable inputs from empirical data, while instruments may also contain observable components hedged with Level 1 or 2 positions. It describes how reported input ranges and averages are calculated and cautions that they reflect instrument characteristics, not uncertainty or estimate reasonableness. A 2024 table lists Level 3 instruments, fair values, techniques, and unobservable-input ranges and averages; notes explain aggregation, instrument composition, structured notes, equity valuation, price conventions, and averaging methods.

nodes.title: Changes in and ranges of unobservable inputs

nodes.title: Credit & funding adjustments & Assets and liabilities measured at FV on a nonrecurring basis
key_items: Valuation adjustments on fair value option elected liabilities
nodes.summary: Derivative fair values are adjusted for counterparty credit risk (CVA) and funding costs (FVA) when market participants would consider them. CVA uses expected exposure, default probabilities from CDS spreads, estimated recoveries, and mitigants such as collateral and offset rights. FVA for uncollateralized or partly collateralized OTC derivatives reflects expected funding needs and market funding costs, including the Firm’s credit risk on liabilities; collateralized derivatives use OIS discounting and need no separate FVA. The text reports 2022–2024 CVA and FVA impacts on principal transactions revenue, excluding related hedges, and explains that fair value option liabilities’ DVA reflects changes in default probability and loss given default inferred from bond spreads: realized gains or losses go to principal transactions revenue, unrealized amounts to OCI.

It details the Firm’s Visa B-2 holdings, 2024 exchange offer, Visa C share gains and disposal, conversion restrictions and uncertainty, and related derivatives. nodes.title: Note 4 - Credit risk concentrations
nodes.summary: The note defines credit-risk concentrations and describes JPMorganChase’s monitoring, senior-management oversight, collateral practices, and controls: consumer risks are assessed by product and U.S. region, while wholesale risks are assessed by industry and client. nodes.title: Note 5 - Derivative instruments
Derivative Activities, Risk Management, and Clearing
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase uses derivatives primarily for client market-making and to manage its own risks. It offsets client exposures and uses interest rate, foreign currency, commodity, and credit derivatives to hedge related risks, with gains or losses expected to substantially offset changes in assets, liabilities, transactions, or inventory. Contracts are traded bilaterally OTC, exchange-traded and cleared, or OTC-cleared through central counterparties. The Firm also clears client derivatives as a clearing member but does not record those contracts in its consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Accounting for derivatives

nodes.summary: The Firm records all free-standing derivatives executed for its own account on the consolidated balance sheets at fair value. Under U.S. GAAP, derivative assets and liabilities and related cash collateral may be offset when a legally enforceable master netting agreement exists. Changes in derivative value are accounted for based on hedge designation and qualification; derivatives not designated as hedges are measured at fair value through earnings. Related tabular disclosures and references to notes on offsetting and embedded derivatives in structured notes are provided.

nodes.title: Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes derivative counterparty credit risk and its use of enforceable netting and collateral agreements to mitigate it, while derivative payables create liquidity risk through collateral requirements and potential termination following credit-rating downgrades. Tables report 2024 and 2023 net payables with downgrade features and collateral posted, plus estimated additional collateral and termination-settlement amounts for single- and two-notch downgrades; downgrade effects generally require breaching the contract’s rating threshold. nodes.title: Derivatives designated as hedges
Liquidity risk and credit-related contingent features
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase explains that derivative receivables create counterparty credit risk, mitigated where possible by enforceable netting and collateral agreements, while payables can create liquidity needs from collateral calls or downgrade-triggered termination. At year-end 2024 and 2023, it reports net OTC and OTC-cleared derivative payables with downgrade features and collateral posted, plus estimated additional collateral and settlement amounts under one- and two-notch downgrades; triggers generally depend on falling below the contract’s lowest referenced agency rating. It also describes asset transfers paired with derivatives: generally treated as collateralized financings, with sale accounting in limited cases; such outstanding sale-accounted transfers were immaterial at both year-ends.

nodes.title: Credit derivatives
Credit default swaps
nodes.summary: Credit derivatives transfer third-party credit risk from protection purchasers to sellers, who earn premiums but assume losses after events such as bankruptcy, nonpayment, or restructuring; purchasers also bear seller credit risk. The Firm both buys and sells protection, acting as a customer-serving market-maker and managing lending, counterparty, and market-making credit exposures. CDS may reference a single entity, an index, or a specified portfolio or tranche; they can be OTC or cleared. Indices periodically update their constituents, removing entities after credit events. At settlement, purchasers claim the difference between contract face value and the reference obligation’s recovery value from the seller, without needing to own the underlying debt.

nodes.title: Credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Credit-related notes are funded derivatives through which investors provide par upfront in exchange for periodic credit-linked payments and par repayment at maturity, unless a specified reference-entity credit event triggers settlement at par less the defaulted obligation’s fair value; neither party has recourse to the defaulting entity. The text introduces tables of credit derivative and note notionals sold and purchased at year-end 2024 and 2023, explains that protection sellers typically pay less than full notional after recoveries, and describes the Firm’s hedging and categories of related protection purchased. The Firm does not use notional amounts as its primary risk measure because they omit event probability, recovery value, and related instruments and hedges.

nodes.title: Total credit derivatives and credit-related notes
nodes.summary: Tables compare 2024 and 2023 credit derivatives and credit-related notes (in millions), showing protection sold, purchased against identical underlyings, net protection, other protection purchased, and maximum payout/notional amounts. Notes define other derivatives, credit-related notes, identical-underlying protection, net settlement treatment, and other protection purchased, including coverage of retained lending exposures. nodes.title: Protection sold – credit derivatives ratings (a) /maturity profile December 31, 2024 (in millions)

Ratings are primarily based on S&P and Moody’s; fair values are before legally enforceable master netting agreements, including cash-collateral netting.

Tables detail protection sold by reference-entity rating and maturity, gross and net fair values, and related rating, settlement, and netting conventions.

Describes JPMorganChase’s use of derivatives for client market-making and risk management, trading and clearing arrangements, fair-value accounting, hedge designations and effectiveness, and 2022–2024 notionals, receivables, payables, netting and collateral. Covers counterparty credit and liquidity risks, downgrade-triggered collateral and termination features, and asset transfers. Reports gains and losses for fair-value, cash-flow, net-investment and portfolio hedges, non-designated risk-management derivatives, and market-making activities, including income and OCI effects, hedge exclusions and AOCI reclassifications. Explains credit derivatives and related notes, protection bought and sold, potential payouts, fair values, ratings, maturities, settlement and limitations of notional amounts as a risk measure.

nodes.title: Note 6 - Noninterest revenue and noninterest expense
Noninterest revenue
Investment banking fees

nodes.title: Principal transactions
nodes.summary: The note explains recognition of noninterest revenue, including demand-terminable customer contracts and fixed-term obligations tied to future events. It details investment banking underwriting, loan syndication and advisory services, with 2022–2024 fee totals and CIB attribution. Principal transactions cover trading spreads, realized and unrealized gains and losses, market-making, hedging and commodity activities; instrument-level revenue and totals are shown for 2022–2024, with exclusions and valuation footnotes. Lending- and deposit-related fee types, recognition, annual amounts, an acquired-commitment discount adjustment and business-line attribution are presented. Asset-management fee types, recognition, annual amounts and attribution are described, as are brokerage, custody and other commissions, their recognition and net presentation of certain costs.

nodes.title: Trading, Lending, Deposit, and Asset Management Revenue
nodes.summary: The page reports trading revenue by instrument, private equity gains or losses, and principal transactions for 2022–2024, with valuation-adjustment and markdown notes, and identifies CIB as the primary earner. It explains lending and deposit fee sources, recognition, related commitment references, and 2022–2024 amounts, including First Republic discount amortization; fees are earned by CCB, CIB, and AWM. It describes asset management fee sources and recognition, reports 2022–2024 components, and notes AWM and CCB as primary earners.

nodes.title: Commissions and other fees
nodes.summary: Commissions and other fees include brokerage and custody-related services and other products. Brokerage commissions are recognized when client securities or financial-instrument transactions occur, net of certain third-party clearing-house and exchange costs. Administration fees for custody, fund services, securities lending, and securities clearance are recognized as services are provided. Revenue totaled $7.530 billion in 2024, $6.836 billion in 2023, and $6.581 billion in 2022. Brokerage commissions and fees were $3.119 billion, $2.820 billion, and $2.831 billion; administration fees were $2.526 billion, $2.310 billion, and $2.348 billion; and all other commissions and fees were $1.885 billion, $1.706 billion, and $1.402 billion, respectively. Other fees include annuity sales commissions, depositary receipt services, travel-related sales commissions, and other service fees, recognized when rendered. These revenues are earned primarily by CIB, CCB, and AWM.

nodes.title: Mortgage fees and related income
nodes.summary: Mortgage fees and related income comprise home-loan production revenue (origination, sales, valuation and pipeline risk-management effects) and servicing revenue (third-party servicing, MSR valuation and risk management, securitization and certain repurchased-loan effects); mortgage-loan interest is reported as interest income. Card income includes transaction interchange and merchant processing, plus deferred account-origination costs and annual fees amortized over 12 months. Proprietary rewards costs reduce card income. Co-brand partner payments are classified as marketing expense, reductions of card income, or deferred origination costs depending on their purpose. Card income totaled $5.497 billion in 2024, $4.784 billion in 2023 and $4.420 billion in 2022; components include interchange/processing, reward costs and partner payments, and other items. Income is earned primarily by CCB and CIB.

nodes.title: Card income
nodes.summary: The text reports commissions and other fees for 2022–2024, broken down into brokerage, administration, and other fees, noting their principal business sources and examples of other fees. It explains mortgage fees and related income, including production, servicing, fair-value and risk-management components, and where mortgage-loan interest is reported. It describes card income recognition, rewards liabilities and costs, and co-brand partner agreements and payment accounting. A table gives card income components and totals for 2022–2024; card income is earned mainly by CCB and CIB.

nodes.title: Other income
nodes.summary: Other income includes operating lease income and losses on tax-oriented investments, mainly CIB alternative-energy equity-method investments; associated tax credits more than offset those losses through lower tax expense. Reported components for 2024, 2023 and 2022 include lease income ($2,795 million, $2,843 million and $3,654 million) and investment losses ($97 million, $1,538 million and $1,491 million), plus Visa-related gains, a First Republic bargain purchase gain and a CIFM acquisition gain in applicable years. Notes explain the Visa and CIFM gains and refer to operating-lease disclosures. From January 1, 2024, new proportional-amortization guidance shifted certain investment amortization from other income to income tax expense, aligning it with related tax credits and benefits.

Covers noninterest revenue sources, recognition policies, 2022–2024 amounts, components, and primary business-line attribution. Topics include investment banking underwriting, loan arrangement and syndication, and advisory fees; principal trading revenue and gains or losses across financial and commodity markets; lending, deposit, and asset-management fees; brokerage, custody, and other commissions; mortgage production and servicing income; and card interchange, processing, rewards, and partner payments. It also details operating lease income, tax-oriented investment losses, acquisition- and Visa-related gains, and the 2024 accounting change for certain investment amortization.

nodes.title: Noninterest expense Other expense

Also presents other expenses for 2022–2024, including legal, FDIC, operating-loss, Visa Foundation contribution, and First Republic integration, restructuring, and FDIC-payment costs, with references to related notes.

nodes.title: Note 7 - Interest income and Interest expense

Discounts and premiums are generally amortized using a level yield, with certain callable-security premiums amortized to the earliest call date. HTM securities were all investment grade, current and accruing at year-end 2024 and 2023, with about 99% rated AA+ or higher. Presents portfolio balances, fair values, unrealized losses by age and type, credit ratings, allowance methods and balances, and realized results and provisions for 2022–2024. nodes.title: Note 11 - Securities financing activities
key_items: Transfers not qualifying for sale accounting

It describes collateral and counterparty risk controls and presents 2024 and 2023 gross, netted, non-nettable, and net balances; collateral asset types; and repurchase and securities-lending maturities. It also reports securities-for-securities lending treatment and transferred assets that did not qualify for sale accounting, recorded as collateralized financings.

nodes.title: Note 12 - Loans
Loan accounting framework
key_items: Interest income; Allowance for loan losses
nodes.summary: The note explains loan accounting by strategy: held-for-investment, held-for-sale, or fair value. It covers amortized-cost measurement, interest and fee recognition, nonaccrual criteria and treatment, expected-credit-loss allowances, and consumer and wholesale charge-off rules, including collateral valuation and appraisal practices. Held-for-sale loans are measured at lower of cost or fair value, while fair-value-option loans are measured at fair value; both recognize interest contractually, are subject to nonaccrual policies, and are excluded from allowance and charge-off policies.

nodes.title: Loan classification changes
nodes.summary: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value; credit losses reduce the allowance, while other losses enter noninterest revenue. Loans retained in held-for-sale return to held-for-investment at amortized cost and are assessed for impairment. The Firm modifies loans for financially troubled borrowers through concessions to limit losses and avoid foreclosure or repossession. Most modified loans other than credit cards enter nonaccrual status and may resume accrual after at least six months or payments of performance and reasonable repayment assurance; limited current loans remain accruing. Allowances for modified loans use established methods that consider expected defaults.

nodes.title: Foreclosed property
nodes.summary: The Firm acquires real estate and other commercial or personal property through loan restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures. It recognizes property when received in satisfaction of a loan, generally at a foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu transaction for real estate. Foreclosed assets are reported in other assets at fair value less estimated selling costs, reviewed quarterly, and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value; subsequent valuation changes affect noninterest revenue, while operating costs such as taxes and maintenance are charged to other expense.

nodes.title: Loan portfolio
nodes.summary: The Firm divides loans into Consumer (excluding credit card), Credit card, and Wholesale segments, monitoring risk by loan class: residential real estate and auto/other; credit card loans; and wholesale real-estate-secured, commercial and industrial, and other loans. Notes define the included businesses and borrowers. Tables report retained, held-for-sale, fair-value, and total loan balances for 2024 and 2023, with accrued-interest and accounting-basis exclusions. Separate 2024 and 2023 tables show retained-loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale, excluding reclassified loans sold subsequently.

nodes.title: Credit card
key_items: Gains and losses on sales of loans

It reports retained, held-for-sale, fair-value, and total loan balances at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including accrued-interest and carrying-value qualifications. It summarizes loan purchases, sales, and reclassifications to held-for-sale for 2022–2024, explaining noncash reclassifications, Ginnie Mae repurchases, excluded correspondent-channel purchases, and First Republic acquisition loans. nodes.title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: Consumer loans excluding credit cards are primarily scored prime-market residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines, auto, and business banking loans, including junior-lien, interest-only, and some negative-amortization products. Retained balances fell from $397.3 billion in 2023 to $376.3 billion in 2024; residential real estate declined from $326.4 billion to $309.5 billion, and auto and other from $70.9 billion to $66.8 billion. Delinquency rates indicate credit quality; over-30-day delinquencies provide early warning, while residential delinquencies over 150 days signal potential foreclosure or liquidation. Residential risk assessment also considers current LTV or combined LTV, collateral geography, and refreshed FICO scores; high LTV and low FICO together indicate greater default risk. Geographic distribution also informs scored auto and business banking loan performance.

nodes.title: Residential real estate
nodes.summary: The section reports retained residential mortgage credit quality for 2024 and 2023, including delinquency by origination year and loan type, 30+-day delinquency ratios, gross charge-offs, lien mix and why converted revolving loans are more delinquent. It details nonaccrual balances, current LTV/FICO categories, geographic exposure, measurement methods and related accounting disclosures. It describes financially distressed modifications (FDMs), their terms and financial effects, payment status, defaults and trial modifications; legacy 2022 TDR volumes, concessions, effects and defaults; and loans in active or suspended foreclosure.

nodes.title: Residential Real Estate TDRs: Nature and Financial Effects
key_items: Financial effects of TDRs and defaults
nodes.summary: Before January 1, 2023, qualifying concessions to financially troubled residential mortgage borrowers were reported as TDRs; short-term or insignificant changes were excluded. In 2022, new TDRs totaled $362 million, with no additional lending commitments. Programs offered rate reductions, extensions, payment deferrals, forgiveness, and other concessions. The page reports 3,902 trial approvals and 4,182 permanent modifications, concession percentages, and permanent-modification effects: rates fell from 4.75% to 3.35%, extended terms from 22 to 38 years, $1 million in charge-offs, $16 million deferred, $2 million forgiven, and $147 million in loans defaulting within one year.

nodes.title: Credit card loan portfolio
key_items: Financial effects of TDRs and defaults

nodes.title: Wholesale loan portfolio
Wholesale loan portfolio (intro)
nodes.summary: Wholesale loans serve corporations, institutions, small businesses and affluent individuals. Internal risk ratings—based on probability of default, loss given default, borrower finances, repayment sources, contingencies, management, industry and geography—are the primary credit-quality measure and are regularly reviewed. Ratings broadly align qualitatively with S&P/Moody’s; BBB-/Baa3-equivalent or better is generally investment grade. Non-investment-grade loans are classified as noncriticized or criticized, with criticized loans split into performing and nonaccrual; criticized status follows regulatory categories. nodes.title: Total retained loans Gross charge-offs
