Tables break term loans down by origination year and show revolving loans, including loans converted to term loans, with totals. “Other” includes loans to financial institutions, SPEs, personal investment companies and trusts, individuals and entities (primarily private-bank clients), government bodies, and nonprofits; SPE details are referenced in Note 14.

nodes.title: Total retained loans Gross charge-offs
nodes.summary: The excerpt presents retained loan risk ratings by origination year for commercial and industrial and other loan portfolios at December 31, 2024 and 2023, including investment- and noninvestment-grade balances, totals, and gross charge-offs; “other” portfolio categories are defined in a footnote. It also describes real-estate-secured loans, including multifamily, other commercial, criticized and criticized-nonaccrual balances and ratios, and construction and development lending, then introduces geographic distribution and delinquency data for retained wholesale loans.

nodes.title: Loans by geographic distribution (a)
nodes.summary: The tables report retained loan balances by U.S. and non-U.S. borrower domicile, alongside delinquency and criticized/nonaccrual categories, for multiple periods. U.S./non-U.S. classification is based predominantly on borrower domicile; certain 90+-day-past-due loans remain accruing because they are well collateralized. A second table details 2024 and 2023 wholesale nonaccrual loans by real estate, commercial and industrial, and other categories, split between loans with and without allowances. Loans may require no allowance when discounted cash flows or collateral cover amortized cost, often after charge-offs or payments. Cash-basis interest income on nonaccrual loans was $51 million in 2024 and $19 million in 2023.

nodes.title: Total retained loans
nodes.summary: The excerpt details JPMorgan Chase’s retained wholesale real-estate-secured loans, including multifamily and other commercial balances, criticized/nonaccrual measures, construction and development lending, and geographic distribution and delinquency by loan class for 2024 and 2023. It reports nonaccrual balances with and without allowances and related cash-basis interest income. It also describes financial-difficulty modifications (FDMs) by loan class and year, their balances, proportions, effects and payment status, defaults, and unfunded commitments on modified loans.

nodes.title: Nature and extent of TDRs
nodes.summary: Before January 1, 2023, certain modifications to loans for financially distressed borrowers were classified as TDRs, excluding insignificant modifications without concessions and loans covered by the Firm’s CARES Act election to suspend TDR accounting. New TDRs totaled $801 million in 2022, mainly reflecting maturity extensions and covenant waivers in Commercial and Industrial loans; their impact was not material. After the TDR assessment requirements were eliminated, the population of loans classified as FDMs became larger than the former TDR population.

Explains wholesale lending and internal credit-risk ratings, investment-grade classifications, criticized loans, and portfolio diversification. Presents 2024 and 2023 retained-loan balances, risk ratings, and gross charge-offs by loan type, origination year, and revolving status; describes real-estate lending, geographic distribution, delinquency, nonaccrual loans, allowances, and cash-basis interest income. Also covers financial-difficulty modifications, their effects, payment status, defaults and commitments, and the former TDR rules and 2022 activity.

The note explains loan accounting by classification, including measurement, interest and fee recognition, nonaccrual, credit-loss allowances, charge-offs, transfers between held-for-investment and held-for-sale, and troubled-borrower modifications. It covers recognition and valuation of foreclosed property; portfolio segments, loan balances, purchases, sales, reclassifications, and sale gains or losses; and detailed consumer, credit-card, and wholesale portfolio disclosures on composition, delinquencies, credit quality, geography, ratings, charge-offs, nonaccruals, allowances, modifications, defaults, foreclosures, and related accounting and risk practices.

nodes.title: Note 13 - Allowance for credit losses
Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
nodes.summary: The note explains the Firm’s credit-loss allowance components, balance-sheet and income-statement presentation, quarterly executive review, and the judgment and uncertainty involved. It describes expected-life estimates, treatment of cancellable commitments and accrued interest, and collective versus individual assessments and their relevant risk characteristics. Portfolio estimates use five macroeconomic scenarios, credit models, and management adjustments; individual assessments use collateral values or discounted expected cash flows, including loan modifications. Other amortized-cost assets are assessed using historical losses and current conditions; collateral-maintenance exposures generally need no allowance unless borrower or collateral risks warrant one.

nodes.title: Allowance for credit losses and related information
key_items: Discussion of changes in the allowance
nodes.summary: The text presents 2022–2024 allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments, related balances and commitments, and impairment-methodology breakdowns by consumer, card and wholesale portfolios. Notes explain accounting adoption, additional receivables allowances, collateral-dependent loans, balance-sheet classification, and commitments excluded from coverage. It reports the 2024 allowance of $26.9 billion, up $2.1 billion year over year, describing consumer and wholesale drivers, scenario weighting and downside risks, adverse-scenario unemployment and GDP effects, central-case economic forecasts for 2024 and 2023, and references for future estimate updates and further disclosures.

Explains allowance methodology, presentation and quarterly review, including uncertainty, expected-life estimates, cancellable commitments, accrued interest, collective and individual assessments, macroeconomic scenarios, credit models and management adjustments. Covers collateral-based and discounted-cash-flow assessments, modified loans, other amortized-cost assets and collateral-maintenance exposures. Presents 2022–2024 allowance and related balance and commitment data, impairment breakdowns, accounting and classification notes, exclusions, and the 2024 allowance of $26.9 billion—up $2.1 billion—with portfolio drivers, scenario weights, downside risks and economic forecasts.

nodes.title: Note 14 - Variable interest entities
Significant Firm-sponsored VIEs
Credit card securitizations
nodes.summary: Note 14 outlines the Firm’s VIE accounting policies and defines Firm-sponsored VIEs, then lists major types and activities by segment, including credit card, mortgage and other securitizations, conduits, and municipal bond vehicles. It notes AWM’s VIE fund sponsorship and possible consolidation, Corporate’s generally unconsolidated VIE-related investments, and CIB’s dealings with third-party-sponsored VIEs. For credit card trusts, it describes securitization, the Firm’s servicing and retained interests, consolidation as primary beneficiary, asset ring-fencing, a generally 5% minimum interest, and year-end undivided interests of $6.6 billion in 2024 and $4.9 billion in 2023.

nodes.title: Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts
key_items: Residential mortgage; Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
nodes.summary: The text describes the Firm’s sponsored mortgage and other securitizations, retained interests, servicing roles, consolidation judgments, and maximum loss exposure. Tables compare 2024 and 2023 principal amounts of assets in consolidated and nonconsolidated securitization VIEs and the Firm’s interests, with exclusions and credit-rating details. It explains residential mortgage and commercial/consumer securitization practices and consolidation criteria. It also covers re-securitizations, including transfer volumes for 2022–2024, client-shared decision-making, nonconsolidation rationale, holdings in nonconsolidated VIEs, and the absence of consolidated agency or private-label re-securitization VIEs.

nodes.title: Multi-seller conduits
nodes.summary: Multi-seller conduits are bankruptcy-remote entities that finance customers using asset-backed commercial paper, supported by seller/third-party credit enhancements and JPMorgan Chase deal-specific liquidity plus program-wide liquidity and credit enhancement. The Firm consolidates conduits it administers because it directs significant activities and has potentially significant economic interests. It may invest in their paper, but is not generally obligated to buy it; reported holdings were $2.9 billion in 2024 and $9.8 billion in 2023. Lending-related unfunded commitments were $10.3 billion and $10.8 billion, respectively. Municipal bond (TOB) trusts finance bond investments by issuing puttable floating-rate certificates and inverse-floating residuals; residual holders distinguish customer from non-customer trusts. The Firm sponsors non-customer trusts, may provide trust services, and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC may remarket floaters and set their periodic rates.

nodes.title: Municipal bond vehicles
nodes.summary: The notes report interests in nonconsolidated U.S. GSE and government-agency re-securitization VIEs of $3.219 billion in 2024 and $3.371 billion in 2023; none were consolidated, nor were Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs. They describe multi-seller conduits’ asset-backed commercial-paper funding, seller credit enhancements, JPMorgan liquidity and credit support, and why the Firm consolidates conduits it administers. Conduit paper holdings ($2.9 billion and $9.8 billion) were eliminated in consolidation; purchases were not driven by market illiquidity, and the Firm generally has no purchase obligation beyond risk-retention rules. Related unfunded client commitments were $10.3 billion and $10.8 billion. The text also explains municipal tender-option-bond trusts, their floaters and residuals, Firm services and conditional liquidity-provider exposure, and why the Firm consolidates non-customer trusts it sponsors and retains residuals in.

Describes Firm-sponsored VIE accounting, major VIE activities by business segment, and consolidation judgments. Covers credit card trusts, servicing, retained interests, ring-fencing, and reported interests; mortgage and other securitizations, re-securitizations, holdings, exposures, and consolidation criteria; multi-seller conduits, their funding and credit/liquidity support, Firm holdings and commitments; and municipal bond tender-option-bond trusts, their securities, Firm services and exposures, and consolidation of sponsored non-customer trusts.

nodes.title: Consolidated VIE assets and liabilities
nodes.summary: The table reports assets and liabilities of JPMorganChase’s consolidated VIEs by program type for December 31, 2024 and 2023, including trading assets, loans, other assets, total assets, beneficial interests in VIE assets, other liabilities, and total liabilities. Footnotes explain included residential mortgage securitizations and consumer loans; asset and liability scope, settlement and consolidation treatment; balance-sheet classifications and limited recourse for beneficial-interest holders; long-term beneficial interests of $5.5 billion in 2024 and $3.1 billion in 2023; and the classification of other liabilities.

nodes.title: VIEs sponsored by third parties
nodes.summary: The Firm’s transactions with third-party-sponsored VIEs are arm’s-length and generally not consolidated when it lacks significant decision-making power or a potentially significant variable interest; positions are reported like other third-party transactions. It does not consolidate tax credit partnerships controlled by third parties, where it invests as a limited partner and receives tax benefits. Maximum loss exposure was $35.2 billion in 2024 ($15.0 billion unfunded) and $35.1 billion in 2023 ($14.7 billion unfunded); project assessments and withheld capital mitigate risk. The 2024 adoption of expanded proportional-amortization guidance, its eligibility, accounting treatment, and reevaluation requirements are described; no significant triggering events occurred. A table reports program carrying values, tax benefits, amortization losses, and other returns for 2022–2024, with related financial-statement classifications and exclusions. For customer municipal bond TOB trusts, the Firm provides services and may offer liquidity with recourse to residual holders, does not protect them from bond losses, and does not consolidate the trusts. Maximum liquidity exposure was $5.8 billion in 2024 and $5.1 billion in 2023; trust assets were $8.1 billion and $7.3 billion, respectively.

nodes.title: Loan securitizations
nodes.summary: The Firm securitizes and sells residential mortgages, credit card receivables, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans to meet investor demand and generate liquidity. When it need not consolidate a trust, it records a transfer as a sale if the assets are legally isolated from its creditors, the transferee can pledge or exchange them, and the Firm does not retain effective control. For qualifying sales, gains or losses reflect proceeds received—including cash, beneficial interests, or servicing assets—compared with the assets’ carrying value, and are reported as noninterest revenue.

nodes.title: Securitization activity
nodes.summary: Reports 2022–2024 activity for unconsolidated, Firm-sponsored securitizations with sale accounting: principal securitized, cash proceeds, servicing fees, and cash flows on retained interests, with scope notes and exclusions. Provides weighted-average life and discount-rate assumptions for newly originated residential and commercial/other retained interests. Describes nonrecourse mortgage-loan and excess-MSR sales to U.S. GSEs and Ginnie Mae transactions, related proceeds and gains/losses, guarantees, limited shared credit risk, and references to indemnifications and MSR disclosures. Explains options to repurchase delinquent government-backed loans and presents 2024–2023 balances for loans repurchased or eligible for repurchase, real estate owned, and foreclosed guaranteed mortgages.

nodes.title: Loan delinquencies and liquidation losses
nodes.summary: The table reports components, 90-days-past-due amounts, and net liquidation losses or recoveries for loans in Firm-sponsored private-label securitizations where the Firm had continuing involvement, as of or for 2024 and 2023. Total securitized loans were $178.2 billion in 2024 and $160.9 billion in 2023, across residential prime/Alt-A and option ARMs, subprime, and commercial and other loans. The text notes that servicing-only involvement generally creates loss exposure only when delinquent loans or foreclosed assets must be repurchased due to breaches of representations and warranties.

Covers the Firm’s sponsored and third-party VIEs, including activities, consolidation judgments and criteria, exposures, holdings, commitments, servicing, and liquidity support across credit card, mortgage, conduit, tax-credit, and municipal bond programs. Reports consolidated VIE assets and liabilities for 2024 and 2023, with scope and classification notes. Describes third-party VIE accounting, tax-credit investment returns and risks, and adoption of proportional-amortization guidance. Explains loan securitization sale accounting and reports securitization activity, proceeds, servicing and retained-interest cash flows, assumptions, GSE transactions, guarantees, repurchase exposures, and delinquency and liquidation-loss data.

nodes.title: Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets
Note 15 - Goodwill, mortgage servicing rights, and other intangible assets (intro)
nodes.summary: Goodwill is recognized in business combinations as purchase price minus acquired net assets’ fair value, subject to acquisition-date measurement adjustments within one year. It is allocated to reporting units, not amortized, and tested annually in the fourth quarter or more often when indicators arise. Tables show goodwill by segment and Corporate for 2022–2024 and period changes, including acquisitions and foreign currency adjustments. No impairment occurred in those years. Testing compares reporting-unit fair value with carrying value, using allocated capital plus goodwill and other intangibles as a carrying-value proxy. Fair value is primarily estimated through discounted forecast cash flows and terminal values, with risk-adjusted cost-of-equity discount rates, and cross-checked against comparable-company multiples and Firm market capitalization. Future business, credit, capital, economic, market, regulatory, or cost-of-equity deterioration could reduce fair value and cause material impairment.

nodes.title: Mortgage servicing rights
nodes.summary: The text explains MSRs’ nature, recognition, fair-value accounting and OAS valuation model, including key assumptions and market-data comparisons. It describes interest-rate and prepayment sensitivity and hedging with derivatives and securities. Tables report 2022–2024 MSR balances and activity, valuation changes, fee income, serviced loans and servicer advances, with notes on transactions and advance recoverability; mortgage-fee components and risk-management results; and 2023–2024 assumptions and fair-value impacts from adverse prepayment-speed and spread changes. Sensitivities are isolated and may not be linear or independent.

nodes.title: Other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Other intangible assets are initially recorded at fair value, primarily in business combinations. Finite-lived assets, including core deposit and customer relationship intangibles, are amortized over estimated useful lives; indefinite-lived assets, such as asset management contracts, are not amortized. At year-end 2024 versus 2023, gross carrying values were $3.8 billion versus $4.2 billion, accumulated amortization $879 million versus $994 million, and net finite-lived values $1.7 billion versus $2.0 billion; indefinite-lived values were $1.2 billion in both years. 2024 assets included First Republic-related intangibles and CIFM asset management contracts. Amortization expense was $339 million in 2024 and $315 million in 2023; estimated finite-lived amortization for 2025–2029 is $288 million, $285 million, $284 million, $267 million, and $261 million. Assets are tested annually or when impairment indicators arise, with impairment recognized in other expense.

Covers goodwill recognition, allocation, nonamortization, annual impairment testing, valuation methods, segment balances and changes, and risks that could trigger impairment; no impairment occurred in 2022–2024. Explains mortgage servicing rights accounting, fair-value modeling and assumptions, rate and prepayment sensitivity, hedging, balances and activity, fees, serviced loans, advances, and valuation sensitivities. Describes other intangible assets’ initial measurement, finite- and indefinite-lived categories, 2023–2024 balances, acquisition-related assets, amortization expense and forecasts, and impairment testing.

nodes.title: Note 16 - Premises and equipment
nodes.summary: Premises and equipment comprises land at cost; buildings, leasehold improvements, internal-use software, and furniture and equipment at cost less depreciation or amortization; and operating lease right-of-use assets. Total assets were $32.223 billion at December 31, 2024, versus $30.157 billion in 2023, with amounts shown for land/buildings/leasehold improvements, right-of-use assets, and other equipment; certain right-of-use assets are classified in Other assets. Depreciation and amortization use straight-line methods: buildings and equipment over useful lives, leasehold improvements over the shorter of remaining lease term or useful life, and capitalized software costs after it is ready for use. Useful lives are 10–50 years for buildings and leasehold improvements and 3–10 years for software and equipment. Impairment is assessed when events or circumstances suggest an asset may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: Note 17 - Deposits
nodes.summary: Note 17 reports deposits at December 31, 2024 and 2023, split by U.S. and non-U.S. offices and by noninterest- and interest-bearing status, including amounts measured at fair value under the fair value option for structured notes. Total deposits were $2,406,032 million in 2024 and $2,400,688 million in 2023. It also presents time deposits at or above insured limits ($241,878 million in 2024; $222,841 million in 2023) and 2024 remaining maturities of interest-bearing time deposits by year through after five years, with U.S., non-U.S., and combined amounts.

nodes.title: Note 18 - Leases
nodes.summary: Note 18 describes JPMorganChase’s lessee and lessor accounting and lease data. As lessee, it reports predominantly operating leases, accounting policies for lease terms, liabilities, right-of-use assets, discounting, rental expense and real estate components, plus 2024–2023 balances, weighted-average terms and rates, cash-flow and noncash information, rental expense, future payment schedule, and $887 million of signed, not-yet-commenced commitments. As lessor, it covers auto and equipment lease financing, asset depreciation and income recognition, impairment and residual-value risk management, asset carrying values, income and depreciation for 2024–2022, and future lease receipts.

nodes.title: Note 19 - Accounts payable and other liabilities
nodes.summary: Note 19 describes accounts payable and other liabilities, including brokerage payables to customers and for unsettled security purchases, plus accrued expenses such as compensation, card rewards, merchant servicing, leases, interest, taxes and litigation reserves. Total liabilities were $280.7 billion at December 31, 2024, versus $290.3 billion in 2023; brokerage payables were $153.2 billion and $162.0 billion, and other payables were $127.5 billion and $128.3 billion, respectively. Card rewards liabilities were $14.4 billion and $13.2 billion. These reflect estimated redemption costs, accrue as points are earned, decline upon redemption, and rely on redemption-rate and cost-per-point assumptions; period impacts are recorded in Card Income. Other notes provide details on accrued interest, leases, taxes and litigation.

nodes.title: Note 20 - Long-term debt
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s long-term debt spans currencies, mostly U.S. dollars, and fixed or variable rates; fair-value changes on elected equity-linked/indexed instruments generally affect principal transactions revenue, with DVA unrealized gains or losses in OCI. The note details 2024 and 2023 carrying values by issuer, debt type, maturity and rate, beneficial interests, and related footnotes on First Republic’s Purchase Money Note, secured and fair-value debt, zero-coupon notes, rate calculations, callability, and maturities through 2029. It reports average contractual and derivative-adjusted rates, swaps used to manage rate and currency exposure, subsidiary-debt guarantees, and that unsecured debt has no specified rating- or performance-triggered acceleration, borrowing limits, or collateral requirements.

nodes.title: Note 21 - Preferred stock
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s preferred-stock note describes its 200-million-share authorization, common-stock subordination in liquidation, and outstanding non-cumulative series at year-end 2024 and 2023. It summarizes share counts, carrying values, issue and earliest redemption dates, contractual and floating rates, and declared dividends for 2022–2024, with terms explaining SOFR/CMT references, dividend timing and series rate conversions. Each share has a $10,000 liquidation value and redemption price; aggregate liquidation value was $20.2 billion in 2024. The note reports 2024 Series NN and 2025 Series OO issuances, 2024 redemptions of Series X, FF, Q, R, S and U, and 2025 redemption of Series HH. Redemptions are permitted on or after series-specific dates or after capital-treatment events, subject to Federal Reserve non-objection.

nodes.title: Note 22 - Common stock
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase was authorized to issue 9 billion $1-par common shares in 2024 and 2023. The note reports 2022–2024 share issuances, treasury repurchases and reissuances, and year-end shares outstanding. In June 2024, the Board authorized a new $30 billion repurchase program, following the prior program; annual repurchases and purchase prices are listed, with excise-tax and 2022 suspension disclosures. Repurchases are discretionary, depend on business and regulatory factors, may vary or be suspended, and can use open-market, private or Rule 10b5-1 transactions. About 58.8 million shares were reserved for employee and director plans at year-end 2024.

nodes.title: Note 23 - Earnings per share
nodes.summary: Note 23 explains that basic EPS uses the two-class method, allocating earnings to common stock and participating securities; dividend-bearing unvested RSUs qualify as participating securities but are excluded from diluted shares. Diluted EPS includes contingently issuable shares and uses whichever is more dilutive of the two-class and treasury stock methods; the two-class method was more dilutive in all periods shown. The 2024, 2023 and 2022 table reports net income, preferred dividends, earnings allocated to participating securities, income applicable to common stockholders, weighted-average basic and diluted shares, dilutive awards, and basic EPS of $19.79, $16.25 and $12.10 and diluted EPS of $19.75, $16.23 and $12.09, respectively.

nodes.title: Note 24 - Accumulated other comprehensive income/(loss)
nodes.summary: Note 24 defines AOCI components: after-tax investment-security unrealized gains/losses, foreign-currency translation and related derivatives, excluded fair-value hedge components, cash-flow hedges, defined-benefit pension and OPEB items, and own-credit DVA on fair-value-option liabilities. Tables show component balances and annual movements for 2022–2024, plus pre-tax, tax, and after-tax OCI changes. A footnote details transferred AFS/HTM securities. Other notes explain income-statement reclassifications, translation hedge gains/losses, cross-currency basis-spread accounting, cash-flow hedge presentation, and a 2022 pension-settlement remeasurement that reduced pre-tax AOCI by $1.4 billion.

nodes.title: Note 25 - Income taxes
Effective tax rate and expense
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase describes its consolidated U.S. tax filing and asset-and-liability accounting for current and deferred taxes, valuation allowances, jurisdictional estimation uncertainty, and its 2024 adoption of tax-credit investment guidance. The note reconciles statutory and effective tax rates for 2022–2024, reports current and deferred tax expense by jurisdiction and audit-resolution benefits, and explains tax effects recorded directly in equity from accounting adoptions. It also presents U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income and defines non-U.S. income and GILTI tax recognition.

nodes.title: Results from Non-U.S. earnings
key_items: Note 25 – Income taxes; Effective tax rate and expense; Effective tax rate
Tax effect of items recorded in stockholders’ equity
nodes.summary: Note 25 explains JPMorganChase’s consolidated U.S. tax filing, asset-and-liability accounting for current and deferred taxes, valuation allowances, estimation uncertainties across jurisdictions, and its 2024 adoption of tax-credit investment guidance. It reports effective tax rates of 22.1%, 19.6%, and 18.4% for 2024–2022, with rate-reconciliation factors and a First Republic acquisition footnote; current, deferred, and total tax expense, including audit-resolution benefits; tax effects recorded directly in equity from accounting adoptions; and U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income, with a definition of non-U.S. income and the treatment of global intangible low-tax income.

nodes.title: Deferred taxes
nodes.summary: Deferred tax expense reflects differences between financial-reporting and tax-return values; deferred tax assets are recognized when realization is more likely than not, with allowances for assets deemed unrealizable. The table reports 2024 and 2023 deferred tax asset and liability components, valuation allowances, and net deferred tax assets, including an estimated First Republic acquisition asset. At year-end 2024, tax-attribute carryforward assets were $352 million; disclosed state/local capital losses, U.S. and non-U.S. NOLs, and other federal attributes have varying expiration dates or unlimited carryforward periods. The valuation allowance primarily relates to certain non-U.S. assets, including NOLs.

nodes.title: Unrecognized tax benefits
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s unrecognized tax benefits, excluding interest and penalties, were $6.2 billion, $5.4 billion and $5.0 billion at year-end 2024, 2023 and 2022; amounts that would reduce the effective tax rate if recognized were $4.4 billion, $3.9 billion and $3.8 billion. Some items would not affect the rate because of temporary differences or tax offsets. The Firm assesses positions and ongoing audits, and the gross balance could increase or decrease by about $2.4 billion over the next 12 months, resulting in payment or income-statement recognition. A reconciliation shows balances rising from $5.0 billion in 2022 to $5.4 billion in 2023 and $6.2 billion in 2024, reflecting current- and prior-period position changes and cash settlements. After-tax interest expense and penalties were $288 million, $229 million and $141 million, respectively; accrued related liabilities were $1.7 billion in 2024 and $1.6 billion in 2023.

nodes.title: Tax examination status
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase reports ongoing tax examinations worldwide; at year-end 2024, U.S. years 2011–2020, New York City years 2015–2018, and U.K. years 2017–2022 were under examination at field or appellate stages. Regulatory rules restrict certain cash and assets: restricted cash totaled $27.5 billion in 2024 versus $19.6 billion in 2023, alongside customer-related restricted securities and collateral. Federal law limits secured intercompany transactions, dividends, and credit based on capital, safety, and liquidity requirements. The IHC structure, Parent Company funding sources and obligations are described; banking subsidiaries had about $15.5 billion of dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2025.

Covers JPMorganChase’s tax accounting policies, estimation uncertainties and 2024 adoption of tax-credit investment guidance; effective tax rates and reconciliations, tax expense by jurisdiction, audit-resolution benefits, equity tax effects, and U.S. and non-U.S. pretax income and GILTI. It details deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowances and tax-attribute carryforwards; unrecognized tax benefits, related interest and penalties, and possible changes; and worldwide tax examinations. It also describes restricted cash, securities and collateral, regulatory limits on intercompany transactions and dividends, the IHC structure, Parent Company funding and obligations, and banking subsidiaries’ dividend capacity.

nodes.title: Note 26 - Restrictions on cash and intercompany funds transfers
key_items: Restricted cash and other restricted assets
nodes.summary: The note describes regulatory restrictions on the Firm’s cash and assets, including OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC and non-U.S. requirements. Restricted cash totaled $27.5 billion in 2024 versus $19.6 billion in 2023, including customer-segregated funds and central-bank reserves; other restricted assets included customer-related pledged cash and securities. It also explains legal limits on bank lending and other covered transactions with the Parent Company and affiliates, the IHC’s role and funding flows, regulators’ authority to restrict dividends, IHC distribution limits tied to capital and liquidity thresholds, and approximately $15.5 billion of bank-subsidiary dividend capacity without prior approval at January 1, 2025, supplemented by 2025 earnings.

nodes.title: Note 27 - Regulatory capital
nodes.summary: Explains Federal Reserve and OCC oversight and Basel III Standardized and Advanced risk-weighted capital frameworks, including how compliance is assessed and required CET1, Tier 1, total capital, leverage, and supplementary leverage ratios. Tables give 2024 and 2023 firm and bank requirements, well-capitalized thresholds, buffers, surcharges, and regulatory notes. Describes the phaseout of CECL transition benefits and reports 2024 and 2023 capital, risk-weighted assets, ratios, adjusted average assets, leverage exposure, and leverage ratios under both approaches. Both entities met all requirements and were well-capitalized.

nodes.title: Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
Note 28 - Off-balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments (intro)
nodes.summary: JPMorganChase’s lending-related commitments, guarantees, and other off-balance-sheet instruments support customer financing. Contractual amounts represent maximum potential credit risk but generally do not reflect expected exposure or funding needs, since instruments are often renewed, cancelled, expired, or undrawn without default. The Firm maintains an allowance for expected losses on wholesale and certain consumer commitments (see Note 13). The table reports contractual amounts and carrying values for 2024 and 2023; listed card, home-equity, and certain business-banking commitments show total available credit, which is not expected to be fully used simultaneously. Commitments may be reduced or cancelled as allowed by contract or law, including after borrower credit deterioration or declining collateral values.

nodes.title: Off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and other commitments
nodes.summary: The excerpt reports JPMorgan Chase’s 2024 and 2023 off-balance-sheet lending-related instruments, guarantees and commitments by type, maturity, contractual amount and carrying value, with notes on scope, risk participations, collateral, First Republic fair-value adjustments and accounting treatment. It explains the nature of unfunded credit commitments and U.S. GAAP recognition and amortization of guarantees and contingent obligations, identifies arrangements treated as guarantees, and describes standby letters of credit and financial guarantees. A table gives their investment-grade and noninvestment-grade amounts, carrying values, allowances, guarantee liabilities and collateral-backed commitments.

nodes.title: Credit Commitments and Guarantees
key_items: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
nodes.summary: Describes unfunded credit commitments for working capital, corporate purposes, commercial paper and bond support, clearing liquidity, and multipurpose facilities. Explains U.S. GAAP’s definition and accounting for guarantees, including initial fair-value recognition, amortization, and recognition of lending and non-lending contingent obligations; lists the Firm’s guarantee arrangements and refers to related contractual amounts and carrying values. Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees are conditional commitments backing clients’ obligations in financing, trade, and similar transactions.

nodes.title: Standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and other letters of credit
key_items: Securities lending indemnifications; Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
nodes.summary: The text reports 2024 and 2023 amounts for standby letters of credit, other financial guarantees and letters of credit, including contractual totals by internal credit grade, allowances, guarantee liabilities, carrying values and collateral-backed commitments. It describes securities-lending indemnifications, daily collateralization above 100%, and use of collateral after borrower default, plus indemnification on invested cash collateral. It explains guarantee-like derivatives—written puts and stable value contracts—their purposes, exposure, fair value and hedging, and provides 2024/2023 notionals, limited stable-value exposure and derivative payables. The Firm also buys and sells credit protection.

nodes.title: Unsettled securities financing agreements

nodes.title: Rights Upon Liquidation
nodes.summary: Upon liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, each Listed Preferred Stock series receives $10,000 per share plus declared, unpaid dividends before junior equity; undeclared dividends do not accumulate, and holders have no claim to remaining assets. If funds are insufficient, the series and equally ranked stock share distributions ratably. Asset sales and mergers or consolidations are not deemed liquidation events. As a holding company, the company’s and its stockholders’ claims to subsidiary assets may follow subsidiary creditors’ claims. Preferred holders are subordinate to company debt and other non-equity claims and may be fully subordinated to U.S. government interests in insolvency or similar proceedings.

nodes.title: 1. Summary or Rationale
nodes.summary: Exhibit 19 is JPMC’s firmwide Insider Trading Policy, effective January 31, 2025. It aims to ensure compliance with U.S. securities laws prohibiting trading in Firm Securities while possessing Firm Material Nonpublic Information and improperly tipping others. It applies worldwide, subject to Firm policies, to directors, employees, non-employees, their Connected Persons, and accounts they can influence or control; JPMC and subsidiaries are also barred from such trading. Defined terms include JPMC’s CEO and CFO, a Closed Window Period (any time outside an Open Window Period), and Connected Persons: a Firm Person’s spouse, domestic partner, minor children, financially supported individuals or those whose investment decisions they can influence, and entities they or those individuals control.

nodes.title: 2. Detailed Terms
nodes.summary: Exhibit 19 is JPMC’s firmwide Insider Trading Policy, effective January 31, 2025. It aims to prevent trading in Firm Securities while possessing Firm material nonpublic information (MNPI) and improper tipping. It applies worldwide, subject to Firm policies, to directors, employees, non-employees, their connected persons, relevant accounts, and JPMC and subsidiaries. It defines key roles and terms, including connected persons, Firm Personnel and Securities, MNPI, trading and transactions, open and closed trading windows, Window List Personnel, and qualifying Rule 10b5-1 plans. Open windows generally run from the day after quarterly earnings release through the 15th of the following month and may be suspended.

nodes.title: 3. Prohibition on Insider Trading
nodes.summary: Insider trading is illegal and prohibited. Firm Personnel and Connected Persons, as well as JPMC and its subsidiaries, must not trade in Firm Securities while possessing Firm MNPI. JPMC generally observes blackout periods when it possesses or may be deemed to possess MNPI, but may repurchase common stock under a 10b5-1 Plan during the blackout before quarterly earnings announcements.

nodes.title: 4. Prohibition on Unauthorized Disclosure
nodes.summary:
4. Prohibition on Unauthorized Disclosure
Firm Personnel and their Connected Persons must not impermissibly provide Firm MNPI to any person who may trade on the basis of that information (i.e., “tipping”). In addition, Firm MNPI must not be shared with any person unless the disclosure complies with the Firm’s policies concerning the safeguarding of confidential information, including the Code of Conduct.

nodes.title: 5. Policies applicable to Window List Personnel
nodes.summary: Window List Personnel and Connected Persons may trade Firm Securities only during open windows with Compliance preapproval; trading is barred during closed windows, though rare exceptions may be considered with management, Compliance, and Legal. Approvals are time-limited, and windows may be suspended. Covered transactions include direct trades and gifts, specified plan liquidations, limit orders, 10b5-1 Plan changes, and certain option-exercise share uses; additional equity-award restrictions apply. Listed automatic purchases, approved-plan trades, and certain previously placed orders or derivatives are exempt from preapproval. Non-Window List Personnel generally face no stated preapproval or minimum-holding requirements, though other restrictions may apply. Corporate Officers and Directors must use 10b5-1 Plans for open-market sales; other specified exercises, gifts, and trust transactions require preapproval but not a plan. Plans must meet Rule 10b5-1(c), follow share-retention policies, and be created, amended, or terminated during open windows. Officers and Directors need specified preapproval to trade or enter plans; the excerpt begins a requirement for CEO and General Counsel approval.

nodes.title: 6. Policies applicable to Corp Officers and Directors
key_items: 6.1 Transactions that are Required to be Pursuant to a 10b5-1 Plan
6.2 Pre-approval for Firm Securities Transactions and Entry into 10b5-1 Plans
nodes.summary: The text prohibits using previously owned JPMC shares or share withholding for option exercises, except under an eligible 10b5-1 Plan. It identifies transactions exempt from restrictions and preapproval for Window List Personnel and Connected Persons: qualifying dividend reinvestments and automatic purchases, preapproved 10b5-1 Plan transactions, and orders or derivatives placed during an Open Window but executed during a Closed Window. Corporate Officers and Directors must use a 10b5-1 Plan for open-market sales; specified exercises, gifts, and GRAT-related transactions require preapproval but not a plan. Plans must satisfy Rule 10b5-1(c), comply with share-retention policies, and be entered, amended, or terminated during an Open Window. During Open Windows, required trades and plan actions need designated approvals: generally CEO and GC; GC actions require CEO approval, Firmwide Controller actions GC and CFO approval, and CEO actions GC approval. Officer approvals also go to Compliance, are generally valid through the next business day, and may specify another duration.

nodes.title: 7. Other Prohibitions
nodes.summary: The policy prohibits Window List Personnel and other employees subject to personal-account dealing restrictions from trading Firm Securities through forwards, futures, swaps, uncovered options (except LEAPS), or short sales. Direct hedging is permitted if proportionate and fully covered, but employees may not hedge or pledge unvested JPMC compensation shares. JPMC Operating Committee members and Directors may not pledge or hedge outright or deferred-compensation JPMC shares. Window List Personnel and Connected Persons must meet region- or business-specific minimum holding periods; vested JPMC shares and ESPP-purchased shares are deemed to satisfy them.

nodes.title: 8. Post-termination Transactions
nodes.summary: After ending their Firm relationship, individuals aware of Firm material nonpublic information (MNPI), and their connected persons, must not trade Firm securities or disclose the information until it is public or no longer material. Personnel and connected persons bear sole responsibility for compliance; the policy does not guarantee immunity from legal liability or provide legal advice, and financial emergencies are no excuse. Violations may bring reminders, disciplinary action up to termination (subject to local law), and orders to cancel trades at the individual’s expense. Questions should go to Compliance or the Office of the Secretary; personnel should consult the Code of Conduct and related policies.

nodes.title: 9. Personal Responsibility and Disciplinary Action
nodes.summary: Window List Personnel and Connected Persons must meet region- or business-specific minimum holding periods before trading Firm Securities; vested JPMC shares and ESPP-purchased shares count as satisfying this requirement. After service ends, anyone aware of Firm MNPI must not trade Firm Securities or disclose the information until it is public or no longer material. Individuals remain personally responsible for compliance; the policy does not guarantee legal compliance, provide legal advice, or excuse trading due to financial emergencies. Violations may bring civil or criminal liability, reminders, disciplinary action up to termination, or an instruction to cancel a trade at the individual’s expense. Questions may be directed to Compliance or the Office of the Secretary; personnel should also consult the Code of Conduct and related policies.
